Greek dishes.Moussaka: Layers of aubergine and spiced meat topped with béchamel; the Greek version was shaped by chef Nikolaos Tselementes in the 1920s.
Greek dishes.Souvlaki: Small skewers of grilled meat, one of the most popular street foods in Greece, and it is usually eaten with pita.
Greek dishes.Gyros: Meat roasted on a vertical spit and sliced into pita; the name comes from the Greek word for 'turn'.
Greek dishes.Spanakopita: Spinach and feta pie baked in layers of crisp filo pastry; the filo is brushed with butter or oil between each layer.
Greek dishes.Tzatziki: A cooling dip of strained yoghurt, cucumber and garlic, which Greeks often serve with grilled meats.
Greek dishes.Dolmades: Vine leaves wrapped around rice and herbs; 'dolma' comes from a Turkish word meaning 'stuffed', and the dish is shared around the region.
Greek dishes.Pastitsio: A baked pasta dish with a thick layer of béchamel, often described as the Greek answer to lasagne.
Greek dishes.Saganaki: Named for the small two-handled pan it's cooked in; the cheese is fried until golden, and sometimes flambéed at the table.
Greek dishes.Loukoumades: Fried dough balls soaked in honey syrup, which are said to have been given to winners at the ancient Olympic Games.
Greek dishes.Avgolemono: A silky egg and lemon sauce or soup thickened with eggs, rather than cream, and often with rice or chicken.
Greek dishes.Stifado: A slow-cooked stew of beef or rabbit with lots of small onions, red wine and warm spices.
Greek dishes.Horiatiki: The real Greek 'village salad': tomato, cucumber, onion, olives and a slab of feta, with no lettuce.
Greek dishes.Paella: A Spanish rice dish from Valencia, cooked in a wide pan, and not Greek, though Greek cooks also love rice dishes.
Greek dishes.Risotto: Italian rice stirred slowly with stock until creamy, and not Greek, though Greece has its own rice dish, spanakorizo.
Greek dishes.Shawarma: A Middle Eastern spit-roasted meat dish that is a cousin of Greek gyros, but not Greek.
Greek dishes.Pierogi: Polish filled dumplings, often served with fried onions and sour cream, and not Greek.
Greek dishes.Goulash: A Hungarian stew seasoned with paprika, which began as a herdsmen's meal, and not Greek.
Greek dishes.Tagine: A North African slow-cooked stew, not Greek.
Greek dishes.Lasagne: Italian layered pasta, which has a Greek cousin in pastitsio but is not Greek itself.
Greek dishes.Gnocchi: Italian dumplings of potato and flour, not Greek, and their name may come from the word for knuckle or knot.
Greek dishes.Borscht: A beetroot soup of Ukraine and Eastern Europe, not Greek.
Greek dishes.Ratatouille: A French vegetable stew from Provence, though the Greek dish briam is similar.
Greek dishes.Churros: Spanish fried dough sticks dunked in thick chocolate, not Greek.
Greek dishes.Bruschetta: Italian grilled bread with olive oil, garlic and tomato, not Greek.

Things made from soybeans.Tofu: Soy milk curdled with a coagulant, then pressed, much like cheesemaking. It has been made in China for about two thousand years.
Things made from soybeans.Tempeh: Whole soybeans fermented with a mold into a firm cake. It comes from Indonesia and is held together by white threads of fungus.
Things made from soybeans.Edamame: Young soybeans picked while still green in the pod. In Japan they are a classic pairing with cold beer.
Things made from soybeans.Miso: Fermented soybean paste, often mixed with rice or barley koji. Aged for months or years, darker miso tastes stronger.
Things made from soybeans.Soy sauce: Brewed from fermented soybeans and roasted wheat, then aged. Real brewed versions take months, while cheap ones use quick chemical hydrolysis.
Things made from soybeans.Natto: Fermented soybeans famed in Japan for its sticky strings and strong smell. Many people there eat it for breakfast.
Things made from soybeans.Soy milk: A drink made by grinding and straining soaked soybeans. It has been consumed in China for centuries, long before milk alternatives were trendy.
Things made from soybeans.Yuba: The skin that forms atop heated soy milk, lifted off in sheets. It is prized in Japanese temple cuisine and sold fresh or dried.
Things made from soybeans.Tamari: A Japanese soy sauce made with little or no wheat, a byproduct of making miso. It tastes richer and is often gluten-free.
Things made from soybeans.Doenjang: Korean fermented soybean paste, funkier and saltier than miso. It is the heart of doenjang jjigae stew.
Things made from soybeans.Hummus: Made of chickpeas, not soy. Its name is simply the Arabic word for chickpeas.
Things made from soybeans.Falafel: Deep-fried balls of ground chickpeas or fava beans, never soy. Egypt and Levant both claim the invention.
Things made from soybeans.Seitan: Made from wheat gluten, not soy, though it is just as protein-rich. It is often mistaken for tofu.
Things made from soybeans.Paneer: A fresh Indian cheese made by curdling milk with acid. It is dairy, so it never goes near soy.
Things made from soybeans.Quorn: A meat substitute made from mycoprotein, a fungus grown in fermentation tanks. It is not made from soy.
Things made from soybeans.Dal: Indian dish of split lentils, peas or pulses. Plenty of soy-free protein, and nothing here comes from soybeans.
Things made from soybeans.Tahini: Paste of ground sesame seeds, so no soy. It is the creamy base of hummus and halva.
Things made from soybeans.Almond milk: A drink made from ground almonds and water. Almonds are tree nuts, unrelated to the soybean.
Things made from soybeans.Oat milk: Made by soaking oats and blending them with enzymes that break down starch into sugars, giving it a natural sweetness. No soy involved.
Things made from soybeans.Coconut aminos: A soy-free alternative to soy sauce made from fermented coconut sap. It tastes a bit sweeter and less salty.
Things made from soybeans.Fish sauce: Anchovies fermented with salt for many months. It is a staple in Thai and Vietnamese cooking and is not a soy product.
Things made from soybeans.Ghee: Butter clarified by simmering off its water and milk solids. It is the traditional cooking fat of India and entirely dairy.
Things made from soybeans.Halloumi: Cypriot cheese made from goat and sheep milk, famous for squeaking when you chew it. Its high melting point lets it grill.
Things made from soybeans.Rice milk: Made from milled rice and water, popular with people with nut or soy allergies. It is naturally sweet.

Liqueurs.Kahlúa: Mexican coffee liqueur from Veracruz, made with rum, sugar, and arabica coffee. It is the key to a Black Russian and a White Russian.
Liqueurs.Baileys: The first Irish cream liqueur, launched in 1974, which combines Irish whiskey and cream that stay stable thanks to a homogenizing process.
Liqueurs.Cointreau: Clear French orange liqueur from Angers, made with sweet and bitter peels, and the standard triple sec in many Margaritas.
Liqueurs.Grand Marnier: Cognac blended with bitter orange essence, made since 1880 by a French family; it is its own aged liqueur, a luxury brand.
Liqueurs.Frangelico: A hazelnut liqueur from Piedmont, Italy, whose bottle is shaped like a monk's robe, complete with rope belt.
Liqueurs.Limoncello: Southern Italy's lemon liqueur, from Amalfi Coast lemons, served ice-cold after dinner. Sunny yellow and sweet.
Liqueurs.Chartreuse: Made by Carthusian monks in France to a secret recipe with 130 herbs. It's one of the few liqueurs that gives its name to a colour.
Liqueurs.Drambuie: Scotch whisky blended with heather honey and herbs, said to come from a recipe given to Bonnie Prince Charlie. Its name is Gaelic for 'the drink that satisfies'.
Liqueurs.Sambuca: Italian anise liqueur, drunk with three coffee beans floating on top, called con la mosca, 'with the fly'.
Liqueurs.Triple sec: A clear orange liqueur, less sweet than curaçao and used in many cocktails. Because it's a style rather than a brand, the quality varies a lot.
Liqueurs.Midori: Bright green Japanese melon liqueur that debuted in 1978, and was the essential 1980s drink, with its Midori Splice.
Liqueurs.Chambord: French raspberry liqueur from the Loire Valley, sold in a round bottle with a crown-shaped lid. It's from the Black Raspberry.
Liqueurs.Gin: A trap: gin is a spirit, not a liqueur. It is a distilled drink with juniper and no added sweetness. Liqueurs are sweetened.
Liqueurs.Vodka: A pure spirit, unsweetened and usually flavourless, not a liqueur. Flavoured vodkas are still not sweet liqueurs.
Liqueurs.Rum: A distilled spirit from sugarcane, normally unsweetened. Spiced rum is flavoured, but is still a spirit.
Liqueurs.Tequila: A spirit distilled from blue agave, not a liqueur, although some brands add sweet liqueur-like flavours.
Liqueurs.Whisky: Distilled from grain mash and aged in oak. Not a liqueur, though Drambuie is made from it.
Liqueurs.Cognac: A brandy distilled from white wine in France, a spirit with no added sugar, not a liqueur.
Liqueurs.Mezcal: A trap: this smoky Mexican spirit is distilled from agave, mostly in Oaxaca. It is not sweetened, so it is a spirit, not a liqueur.
Liqueurs.Sake: A trap: Japanese rice wine is brewed, not distilled, and has no added sugar. It is neither a liqueur nor a spirit.
Liqueurs.Port: A fortified wine from Portugal, whose spirit stops the fermentation. It is sweet but it's wine, not liqueur.
Liqueurs.Sherry: A fortified wine from southern Spain, not a liqueur. Its sweet versions are made from wine, not a spirit with sugar.
Liqueurs.Prosecco: Italian sparkling wine, so it's a wine, not a liqueur. It is lower in alcohol and drier than most liqueurs.

Countries the Sahara stretches into.Libya: Almost all of Libya is desert, and it holds sand seas such as Ubari, plus the Acacus mountains with ancient rock art.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Egypt: The Sahara makes up most of its land, which is why nearly everyone lives along the Nile, a thin green ribbon through the desert.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Sudan: The Sahara covers its north, where the Nile cuts through, and the ancient Nubian pyramids there outnumber Egypt's.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Chad: Its northern Tibesti mountains and Bodélé Depression are Sahara; dust blown from the Bodélé fertilises the Amazon rainforest across the Atlantic.

Countries the Sahara stretches into.Mali: The Sahara covers northern Mali, home to Timbuktu, a medieval trading hub and centre of Islamic learning at the desert's edge.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Mauritania: Its Sahara includes the Richat Structure, a giant bullseye-shaped geological dome visible from space, known as the Eye of the Sahara.

Countries the Sahara stretches into.Tunisia: The southern Sahara includes Chott el Djerid, a vast salt flat, and desert locations that served for Star Wars' Tatooine.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Kenya: A trap: Kenya is much further south, straddling the equator with savanna, highlands and Mount Kenya, not the Sahara.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Ethiopia: Mostly highland, with plateaus above 2,000 metres, so it is not Saharan, though the Danakil Depression is among the hottest places on Earth.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Ghana: A West African coastal country in the tropics, with forest and savanna, and far south of the Sahara's reach.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Somalia: Dry and hot, but its deserts belong to the Horn of Africa, not the Sahara, which lies well to the northwest.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Botswana: Its Kalahari is a different desert in southern Africa, and not part of the Sahara, thousands of kilometres north.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Namibia: Home to the Namib, among the oldest deserts on Earth, but far from the Sahara in the southwest of the continent.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Tanzania: East African, with Kilimanjaro and Serengeti, and thoroughly south of the Sahara.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Uganda: Green and lake-filled, containing the source of the Nile at Lake Victoria, nowhere near the Sahara.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Saudi Arabia: Its great deserts, the Empty Quarter among them, are in Asia, and the Sahara ends at the Red Sea in Africa.

Countries the Sahara stretches into.Oman: Its sands, such as the Wahiba, are on the Arabian Peninsula, across the sea from the Sahara.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Angola: Lies in southwestern Africa, where the Namib desert reaches its southern edge, far from the Sahara.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Zambia: A southern African country known for Victoria Falls, with woodland and rivers rather than desert.
Countries the Sahara stretches into.Ivory Coast: A tropical West African country that's the world's biggest cocoa producer, well south of the Sahara.

Landmarks in Japan.Akihabara: Tokyo's electronics district, now the centre of anime, manga and gaming culture, nicknamed Electric Town.

Landmarks in Japan.Taipei 101: Taiwan's skyscraper was the world's tallest from 2004 to 2010, with a giant damper ball that steadies it in typhoons.

Landmarks in Japan.Marina Bay Sands: Singapore's three-towered hotel topped with a ship-like sky park, opened in 2010.
Landmarks in Japan.The Bund: Shanghai's riverside promenade of colonial-era banks, facing the Pudong skyline in China.
Landmarks in Japan.Lotte World: A giant indoor theme park in Seoul, South Korea, among the largest indoor amusement parks in the world.
Landmarks in Japan.Wat Pho: Bangkok's temple holds a 46-metre-long reclining Buddha and is regarded as the birthplace of Thai massage.

Coniferous trees.Pine: Pine nuts, used in pesto, are the seeds of certain pines. Bristlecone pines in California have lived for nearly 5,000 years.
Coniferous trees.Spruce: Spruce wood is prized for violin and guitar tops because it is light, stiff and resonant. Norway spruce is the classic Christmas tree in Europe.
Coniferous trees.Fir: True firs hold their cones upright and shed them in pieces on the branch. Their flat, soft needles distinguish them from spruces.
Coniferous trees.Cedar: Cedar wood contains oils that repel moths, which is why it lines chests and closets. The famous cedars of Lebanon appear on the country's flag.
Coniferous trees.Redwood: Coast redwoods are the tallest trees on Earth, with some over 110 meters. Fog drifting in from the Pacific provides a lot of their water.
Coniferous trees.Sequoia: Giant sequoias are the biggest trees by volume. Their thick, fibrous bark resists fire, and heat actually helps open their cones.
Coniferous trees.Hemlock: The conifer hemlock is harmless, unlike the poisonous plant that killed Socrates. The tree was named because its crushed needles smelled like that weed.
Coniferous trees.Cypress: Bald cypress trees in swamps send up knobby 'knees' from their roots. Despite being conifers, they drop their needles each autumn.
Coniferous trees.Juniper: Juniper 'berries' are really tiny fleshy cones, and they give gin its flavor. The name 'gin' even comes from the Dutch word for juniper.
Coniferous trees.Yew: Almost every part of a yew is poisonous. A drug made from Pacific yew bark, paclitaxel, became an important cancer treatment.
Coniferous trees.Larch: A conifer that drops its needles each autumn after turning gold. Its dense, rot-resistant wood has long been used for boats.
Coniferous trees.Douglas fir: Not a true fir despite its name, it is in its own genus. It is among the tallest trees in North America and a major source of lumber.
Coniferous trees.Monkey puzzle: A Chilean conifer with spiky, scaly leaves, a 'living fossil' whose relatives lived alongside dinosaurs. Its name came from a joke that monkeys couldn't climb it.
Coniferous trees.Oak: A broadleaf tree, not a conifer. Its acorns are the seeds, and a mature oak can drop thousands of them in a good year.
Coniferous trees.Maple: A broadleaf tree whose sap is boiled into syrup, about 40 liters of sap for one liter of syrup. Its leaf is on Canada's flag.
Coniferous trees.Birch: A broadleaf tree with papery white bark. It is one of the first trees to colonize ground cleared by fire or glaciers.
Coniferous trees.Elm: A broadleaf tree. Dutch elm disease, a fungus spread by beetles, wiped out most elms across North America and Europe in the 1900s.
Coniferous trees.Willow: Its bark contains salicin, the natural source that inspired aspirin. It is a broadleaf tree, so it is no conifer.
Coniferous trees.Beech: A broadleaf tree with smooth gray bark. The word 'book' is thought to come from beech, since early writing was carved on beech wood.
Coniferous trees.Poplar: A fast-growing broadleaf tree. The quaking aspen is a poplar, and a grove can be one organism sharing a single root system.
Coniferous trees.Palm: Palms are flowering plants related to grasses, not conifers. Some are the largest-leaved plants known, with fronds up to 25 meters long.
Coniferous trees.Eucalyptus: An Australian broadleaf, and the only food of koalas. Its oily leaves are flammable, and some species need fire to release their seeds.
Coniferous trees.Holly: A broadleaf evergreen: it keeps its leaves but isn't a conifer. Only female plants bear the red berries, which are toxic to people.
Coniferous trees.Magnolia: Magnolias are among the oldest flowering plants, predating bees. Their flowers evolved to be pollinated by beetles.

Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Maple: Maples are famed for fall color, and the red comes from anthocyanin pigments made in autumn. Syrup comes from the spring sap.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Birch: Birches have thin white papery bark that peels in strips. They're pioneers, quickly colonizing cleared or burnt ground.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Elm: Dutch elm disease devastated elms across Europe and North America during the 20th century. A fungus carried by bark beetles spreads it.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Beech: Beech trees have smooth gray bark that tends to keep carved initials for decades. In autumn, the leaves turn a coppery gold.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Ash: Ash trees are under threat from the emerald ash borer, an invasive beetle. Baseball bats are traditionally made from its strong wood.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Willow: Willow bark was the original source of salicin, which inspired aspirin. These trees love water and root easily from cuttings.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Larch: A conifer that sheds its needles every autumn, which is rare. Its golden fall color lights up mountain forests.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Bald cypress: A conifer that drops its needles in winter, and grows 'knees' sticking up from the roots in swampy water. Some old specimens are over a thousand years old.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Ginkgo: A living fossil, little changed in over 200 million years. Its leaves turn bright yellow and drop almost all at once.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Chestnut: Chestnut blight wiped out billions of American chestnuts in the early 1900s. The tree used to dominate eastern forests.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Poplar: Poplars grow fast and drop their leaves in autumn. Their leaves flutter at the slightest breeze because of their flat stalks.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Aspen: A whole grove can be one organism linked by roots. One in Utah, called Pando, covers about 40 hectares and is thousands of years old.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Sycamore: A deciduous tree with mottled bark that peels in patches. In Europe, the sycamore is a maple, and in North America it is a plane tree.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Pine: Pines are evergreen conifers whose needles last for several years. They shed them gradually, so the tree never looks bare.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Spruce: A spruce keeps its needles year-round. Its wood is prized for violins and guitars for its resonance.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Fir: Firs stay green all year, and many serve as Christmas trees. Their cones stand upright on the branches.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Holly: A broadleaf evergreen with glossy, spiny leaves. It keeps its leaves in winter, and the red berries are toxic to people.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Eucalyptus: An evergreen that sheds bark instead of leaves. Koalas feed on its leaves, which are rich in oils that burn easily.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Redwood: A coast redwood stays green all year and can top 100 meters. These are the tallest trees on Earth.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Yew: An evergreen that can live thousands of years. Almost every part of it is poisonous, though a compound from it is used in cancer drugs.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Cedar: Cedars are evergreens with fragrant, rot-resistant wood. That's why cedar chests and closets are used to protect clothes from moths.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Live oak: Despite being an oak, it's evergreen, replacing leaves gradually in spring. Its name refers to staying green in winter.
Deciduous trees (lose their leaves).Juniper: An evergreen shrub or tree, whose berry-like cones flavor gin. It holds on to its scale-like leaves through the winter.

Parts of the circulatory system.Aorta: The aorta is the body's biggest artery, about as wide as a garden hose, and it carries blood from the heart at high pressure.
Parts of the circulatory system.Atrium: The heart has two atria, the receiving chambers. The word means 'entrance hall' in Latin.
Parts of the circulatory system.Ventricle: The left ventricle has the thickest walls, since it must push blood to the whole body, not just the lungs.
Parts of the circulatory system.Vena cava: The vena cava is the largest vein pair, returning blood to the heart from the head and the body.
Parts of the circulatory system.Pulmonary artery: The pulmonary artery is odd: it is an artery that carries oxygen-poor blood, because arteries are defined by direction, not oxygen content.
Parts of the circulatory system.Capillaries: Capillaries are narrow enough that red cells pass in single file. Laid end to end, the body's capillaries would reach tens of thousands of miles.
Parts of the circulatory system.Veins: Veins return blood to the heart, and many have one-way valves so blood can't flow backward against gravity.
Parts of the circulatory system.Arteries: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, with thick elastic walls. The pulse you feel is a pressure wave in them.
Parts of the circulatory system.Coronary artery: The coronary arteries feed the heart muscle itself. When one is blocked, the result is a heart attack.
Parts of the circulatory system.Carotid artery: The carotid arteries in the neck supply the brain. You can feel a pulse in them just beside the windpipe.
Parts of the circulatory system.Jugular vein: The jugular veins in the neck drain blood from the head. You may see one bulge when you strain.
Parts of the circulatory system.Alveoli: Alveoli are air sacs in the lungs, so they are respiratory. They sit next to capillaries, which carry the blood side.
Parts of the circulatory system.Bronchi: The bronchi are airways leading into the lungs, so they belong to the respiratory system, not circulation.
Parts of the circulatory system.Trachea: The trachea is the windpipe, about 10 cm long, and it carries air to the lungs, not blood around the body.
Parts of the circulatory system.Esophagus: The esophagus is about 25 cm long and moves food to the stomach, so it belongs to digestion, not circulation.
Parts of the circulatory system.Duodenum: The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine, where food meets bile and enzymes, so it is digestive.
Parts of the circulatory system.Colon: The colon is the large intestine's main section, which is digestive, not circulatory.
Parts of the circulatory system.Femur: The femur is the thigh bone, and it is the longest bone. Its marrow makes blood cells, but it's not itself a vessel.
Parts of the circulatory system.Cochlea: The cochlea is a fluid-filled spiral in the inner ear. It handles hearing and not blood flow.
Parts of the circulatory system.Cornea: The cornea is the clear front of the eye. It has no blood vessels at all, which helps it stay transparent.
Parts of the circulatory system.Neuron: Neurons are nerve cells that carry signals. They belong to the nervous system, not the circulatory.
Parts of the circulatory system.Tendon: A tendon joins muscle to bone, and the Achilles is the thickest. It is part of movement, not circulation.
Parts of the circulatory system.Ligament: A ligament joins bone to bone. It stabilises joints and is not part of the circulatory system.
Parts of the circulatory system.Larynx: The larynx is the voice box, part of the airway and the respiratory system, not the circulatory one.

Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Discovered polonium: With Pierre she found polonium in 1898 and named it after Poland, her homeland, then under foreign rule.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Discovered radium: Radium glowed in the dark, and she and Pierre isolated it from tons of ore. Her notebooks are still radioactive today.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Won two Nobel Prizes: She won physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911. She is still the only person to win Nobels in two different sciences.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Coined radioactivity: She introduced the word 'radioactivity' in 1898 to describe the radiation she studied in uranium ores.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.X-ray vans in WWI: She helped equip vehicles nicknamed 'little Curies' that carried X-ray machines to the front, and she drove one herself.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Born in Warsaw: She was born Maria Skłodowska in 1867 in Warsaw, then part of the Russian Empire, and moved to Paris to study.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Taught at Sorbonne: In 1906 she became the first woman professor at the University of Paris, taking over her late husband's teaching post.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.First woman Nobelist: In 1903 she became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, sharing physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Married Pierre Curie: She married Pierre in 1895, and they worked side by side. He died in a street accident in Paris in 1906.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Discovered X-rays: Wilhelm Röntgen found X-rays in 1895, winning the first Nobel in physics. Curie later used them in medicine, but didn't discover them.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Found penicillin: Alexander Fleming found penicillin in 1928. Curie died in 1934, working in a different field of science.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Split the atom: Ernest Rutherford's team split the atom in the early 1900s, with a 1932 landmark by Cockcroft and Walton. Curie didn't.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Geiger counter: Hans Geiger and Rutherford made the detector, and it's named for Geiger. Curie's work involved the electrometer.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Found the electron: J.J. Thomson found the electron in 1897, a year before the Curies' polonium. They studied radiation, not the electron.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Invented dynamite: Alfred Nobel invented dynamite in 1867, and later established the Nobel Prizes that she won.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Discovered DNA: Friedrich Miescher found DNA in 1869, well before Curie began her work. The double helix was solved in 1953.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Born in Paris: She was born in Warsaw, not Paris, and moved to France at 24. She later became a French citizen by marriage.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Relativity: Albert Einstein developed relativity, and he and Curie knew each other, attending the 1911 Solvay Conference together.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Discovered uranium: Martin Klaproth found uranium in 1789. Curie studied its radiation, after Becquerel found it was radioactive in 1896.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Germ theory: Pasteur and Koch built germ theory in the 1800s. Curie worked in physics and chemistry, not microbiology.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Periodic table: Dmitri Mendeleev published his table in 1869. Curie's polonium and radium added new entries to it later.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Discovered helium: Helium was first detected in the Sun's light in 1868, by astronomers Janssen and Lockyer, before it was found on Earth.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Polio vaccine: Jonas Salk's polio vaccine arrived in 1955, decades after Curie's death in 1934.
Marie Curie's real achievements and fact.Steam engine: Steam engines were developed in the 1700s by Newcomen and Watt, long before Curie was born.

Ballroom dances.Waltz: The 3/4 rhythm was once considered scandalous because dancers held each other so close.
Ballroom dances.Foxtrot: It is often credited to vaudeville performer Harry Fox, and it became a craze around 1914.
Ballroom dances.Tango: Born in the port districts of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, the ballroom tango is sharper and more staccato than the original.
Ballroom dances.Quickstep: Developed in the 1920s as a speedy blend of foxtrot and Charleston, it is light, bouncy and full of hops.
Ballroom dances.Cha-cha: The name imitates the sound of dancers' shoes shuffling on the floor. It evolved from Cuban mambo in the 1950s.
Ballroom dances.Rumba: Ballroom rumba is a slow, romantic Latin dance, often called the dance of love, built on Cuban rhythms.
Ballroom dances.Samba: A Brazilian dance with a signature bouncing hip action, rooted in the carnival traditions of Rio.
Ballroom dances.Paso doble: The name means double step in Spanish. The dancers act out a bullfight, with the man as matador and the woman as his cape.
Ballroom dances.Jive: A fast, bouncy Latin ballroom dance descended from American swing and the lindy hop.
Ballroom dances.Viennese waltz: The oldest of the ballroom dances, it spins faster than the regular waltz, at about 60 bars a minute.
Ballroom dances.Breakdance: Born in the Bronx in the 1970s, it is a street dance, and breaking made its Olympic debut at Paris 2024.
Ballroom dances.Tap dance: Dancers make rhythm with metal plates on their shoes. It grew from African and Irish step traditions.
Ballroom dances.Ballet: Developed in Italian Renaissance courts, it still uses French terms. It's a stage art, not a ballroom one.
Ballroom dances.Hula: Hawaiian, so not ballroom. Its hand gestures tell stories, and missionaries tried to suppress it in the 1800s.
Ballroom dances.Macarena: A 1990s party hit, performed in a fixed sequence of arm moves, not as a ballroom partner dance.
Ballroom dances.Limbo: It began in Trinidad as a wake ritual. Dancers bend backward under a lowering pole.
Ballroom dances.Haka: Maori war dance from New Zealand, best known as the pre-match challenge by the All Blacks rugby team.
Ballroom dances.Can-can: A high-kicking cabaret dance from Paris, not a ballroom one, once so scandalous the police tried to restrain it.
Ballroom dances.Moonwalk: Michael Jackson debuted it on TV in 1983, though earlier dancers like Cab Calloway had performed similar slides.
Ballroom dances.Line dancing: Dancers stand in rows doing the same steps, not as couples, and it exploded with country music.
Ballroom dances.Flamenco: The passionate dance and song of Andalusia in Spain, listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage in 2010.
Ballroom dances.Irish jig: A quick Irish folk dance, popularized worldwide by Riverdance in the 1990s.
Ballroom dances.Conga: A Cuban carnival line dance. In 1986, Miami's Calle Ocho conga line set a record with over 119,000 people.
Ballroom dances.Floss: A hip-swinging move made famous by a teenager on Saturday Night Live and by Fortnite in 2018.

Instruments with frets.Guitar: Modern guitars typically have 19 to 24 frets, each a thin metal strip marking where the string must be pressed.
Instruments with frets.Banjo: The banjo's roots lie in West African lutes, brought to America by enslaved people.
Instruments with frets.Mandolin: The mandolin has four pairs of strings tuned like a violin, so violinists can pick it up easily.
Instruments with frets.Ukulele: The word is Hawaiian for 'jumping flea', maybe for the quick fingers of its players.
Instruments with frets.Bass guitar: Leo Fender introduced the electric bass in 1951, and it was easy for upright bass players to carry.
Instruments with frets.Lute: The lute was Europe's favorite instrument in the Renaissance, and it came from the Arabic 'oud'.
Instruments with frets.Sitar: The sitar has movable frets and sympathetic strings that ring on their own, giving its shimmering sound.
Instruments with frets.Bouzouki: The bouzouki is the signature Greek instrument, with a long neck and a metallic sound popular in rebetiko music.
Instruments with frets.Balalaika: The balalaika is a Russian triangular-bodied instrument, usually with three strings.
Instruments with frets.Violin: Trap: violins have no frets, which means players must find each note's position by ear and muscle memory.
Instruments with frets.Viola: Trap: the viola is fretless like the violin, and it needs a precise ear.
Instruments with frets.Cello: Trap: fretless, so a cellist must place fingers exactly, though a viola da gamba has frets.
Instruments with frets.Double bass: Trap: unlike the electric bass, the double bass has no frets, a fretless fingerboard.
Instruments with frets.Harp: Trap: a harp has one string per note, so it needs no frets.
Instruments with frets.Piano: Trap: a piano has keys, not frets, and each note has its own string.
Instruments with frets.Erhu: Trap: the Chinese erhu is a two-string fiddle with no frets.
Instruments with frets.Koto: Trap: the Japanese koto has movable bridges, not frets, for tuning each string.
Instruments with frets.Fiddle: Trap: a fiddle is basically a violin played in folk style, so no frets.
Instruments with frets.Harpsichord: Trap: a harpsichord is a keyboard that plucks strings, and has no frets.
Instruments with frets.Lyre: Trap: the ancient lyre has strings stretched on a frame, and no frets.
Instruments with frets.Trumpet: Trap: a trumpet uses valves to change notes, not frets.
Instruments with frets.Flute: Trap: a flute uses holes and keys, not frets.
Instruments with frets.Xylophone: Trap: a xylophone has wooden bars you strike, not frets.
Instruments with frets.Theremin: Trap: the theremin is played without touching it, by moving hands near two antennas.

Types of drum.Snare drum: The wires stretched across the bottom head give the snare drum its crisp, buzzing crack.
Types of drum.Bongo: Cuban bongos are a joined pair played between the knees, and the smaller drum is called the macho.
Types of drum.Conga: Congas come from Afro-Cuban music and are usually played in sets of two or three, with the hands.
Types of drum.Djembe: A djembe from West Africa is goblet-shaped and carved from a single piece of wood, with a skin head.
Types of drum.Timpani: Timpani are the only orchestral drums tuned to exact notes, and pedals change the pitch quickly.
Types of drum.Tabla: The tabla is a pair of drums: the small right-hand dayan and the bigger bayan, played with fingers and palms.
Types of drum.Bodhrán: The bodhrán is an Irish frame drum, played with a short double-ended stick called a tipper.
Types of drum.Tom-tom: A tom-tom has no snares, and drum kits usually carry several, tuned from high to low.
Types of drum.Taiko: Taiko means simply 'drum' in Japanese, but also names the thunderous ensemble drumming.
Types of drum.Bass drum: The bass drum supplies the kick, and its foot pedal beater was a key invention for the drum kit.
Types of drum.Darbuka: The darbuka is a goblet-shaped drum used across the Middle East, also known as the doumbek.
Types of drum.Cymbal: A cymbal is struck metal, with no drumhead, so it's percussion but not a drum.
Types of drum.Triangle: A triangle is a bent steel rod, with no skin to stretch, so it isn't a drum.
Types of drum.Gong: A gong is a struck metal disc, and without a membrane it isn't a drum.
Types of drum.Maracas: Maracas are rattles filled with seeds or beads, so they're shaken, not struck like drums.
Types of drum.Castanets: Castanets are clappers of wood used in Spanish dance, and they have no drumhead.
Types of drum.Xylophone: A xylophone has wooden bars struck with mallets, with no skin, so it's not a drum.
Types of drum.Marimba: The marimba has wooden bars, much like a deeper xylophone, with no drumhead.
Types of drum.Glockenspiel: The glockenspiel has metal bars, and its name is German for 'bell play'.
Types of drum.Cowbell: A cowbell is a metal bell struck by a stick, not a membrane drum.
Types of drum.Woodblock: A woodblock is a hollowed block of wood that gives a dry knock, so not a drum.
Types of drum.Claves: Claves are two hardwood sticks tapped together, so they're percussion but not drums.
Types of drum.Rainstick: A rainstick is a tube filled with seeds or pebbles, tilted to mimic rain, with no drumhead.
Types of drum.Wind chimes: Wind chimes are tubes or rods ringing in the wind, with no skin stretched over a frame.

Casino games.Blackjack: Card counting isn't illegal, but casinos can ban you for it. The game's best-known hit is a 10-value card plus an ace.
Casino games.Roulette: A standard European wheel has 37 pockets; American wheels add a double zero, which roughly doubles the house edge.
Casino games.Craps: Players bet on the roll of two dice; the game is thought to descend from the English game hazard, and its odds are among the best in the casino.
Casino games.Baccarat: Often the high-roller game of choice, it's famously a game of pure chance: players only choose Player, Banker or Tie.
Casino games.Slot machines: Charles Fey's 1895 'Liberty Bell' in San Francisco is considered the first true slot machine; modern ones are run by random number generators.
Casino games.Keno: This lottery-style game draws 20 numbers from 80, and it's said to descend from a Chinese lottery game of ancient origin.
Casino games.Sic bo: The name means 'dice pair' in Cantonese; players bet on the outcome of three dice, and it's popular in Macau.
Casino games.Texas hold 'em: Each player gets just two private cards plus five shared ones; it became the main event game at the World Series of Poker.
Casino games.Pai gow: Played with Chinese dominoes, players split seven tiles into a two-tile and five-tile hand; many games end in pushes.
Casino games.Three card poker: Invented in the 1990s by Derek Webb as a faster alternative to five-card poker; a straight outranks a flush here.
Casino games.Bridge: A trap: it's played in clubs and living rooms, not casinos, because players compete in partnerships rather than against the house.
Casino games.Canasta: Born in Uruguay in the 1930s, this rummy-style game was a huge craze in 1950s America, but you'll find it at home, not in casinos.
Casino games.Go Fish: A children's card game of asking for matching ranks; with no betting or house edge, casinos have no interest in it.
Casino games.Old Maid: The loser is whoever ends up holding the odd queen; it's a kids' game with no gambling element.
Casino games.Chess: There is no luck involved at all, so casinos don't offer it; its perfect information makes it poor for house-edge gambling.
Casino games.Checkers: Also called draughts, it was proven a draw with perfect play in 2007 after a computer analysis of its trillions of positions.
Casino games.Monopoly: Derived from Elizabeth Magie's 1904 Landlord's Game, which was meant to show how land ownership enriches landlords.
Casino games.Uno: Created in 1971 by Merle Robbins, a barber from Ohio, it was sold from his barbershop before Mattel bought it.
Casino games.Scrabble: Alfred Butts designed it by studying letter frequencies on The New York Times's front page; it's strictly a skill game.
Casino games.Backgammon: Dating back some 5,000 years, it's played for money in many places, but casinos rarely offer it since players compete against each other.
Casino games.Darts: It's a pub game, not a casino one; the standard dartboard's number order was designed to punish inaccurate throws.
Casino games.Pinball: Once banned in New York City as gambling, until a 1976 demonstration proved that flipper skill mattered.
Casino games.Hopscotch: A playground game that goes back to Roman times, when soldiers used longer courts for training.
Casino games.Jenga: Invented by Leslie Scott, who grew up in Africa; its name comes from the Swahili word for 'build'.

Famous soccer players.Mohamed Salah: Liverpool's Egyptian forward has won several Premier League Golden Boots and helped end the club's 30-year wait for a league title in 2020.
Famous soccer players.Wayne Rooney: Manchester United's all-time record scorer with 253 goals, he burst onto the scene as a 16-year-old at Everton.
Famous soccer players.Thierry Henry: Arsenal's all-time top scorer, he won the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000 with France.
Famous soccer players.Michael Jordan: Six NBA titles with the Bulls make him a basketball icon, and he even spent a season playing minor-league baseball.
Famous soccer players.Roger Federer: Won 20 Grand Slam singles titles, eight of them at Wimbledon, in tennis; he never played professional soccer.
Famous soccer players.Tiger Woods: A golfer with 15 majors, he completed a famous comeback by winning the 2019 Masters after years of injuries.
Famous soccer players.Usain Bolt: The sprint star holds the 100m record of 9.58, and in 2018 he trained with an Australian pro soccer club but never signed a contract.
Famous soccer players.Babe Ruth: Baseball's famed slugger hit 714 home runs, and began his career as a star pitcher for the Boston Red Sox.
Famous soccer players.Wayne Gretzky: Ice hockey's 'The Great One' holds so many NHL records that his number 99 was retired across the whole league.
Famous soccer players.Tom Brady: The NFL quarterback won seven Super Bowls, and was once drafted by the baseball Montreal Expos too.
Famous soccer players.Serena Williams: She won 23 Grand Slam singles titles, the most in the modern era of tennis, not soccer.
Famous soccer players.Sachin Tendulkar: India's cricket hero was the first batter to reach 100 international centuries, a record that still stands.
Famous soccer players.Shaquille O'Neal: A 7-foot-1 basketball center who won four NBA titles, he also released rap albums.
Famous soccer players.Jonah Lomu: A giant New Zealand rugby winger whose 1995 World Cup runs flattened defenders; rugby, not soccer.

Famous swimmers.Mark Spitz: At the 1972 Munich Games he won seven golds, each in a world-record time.
Famous swimmers.Katie Ledecky: She holds world records in the 400, 800 and 1500 meter freestyle and has won many Olympic gold medals.
Famous swimmers.Ian Thorpe: Nicknamed The Thorpedo, the Australian was famous for his enormous size 17 feet, which worked like flippers.
Famous swimmers.Ryan Lochte: He has 12 Olympic medals, six of them gold, and was one of Phelps's main rivals.
Famous swimmers.Missy Franklin: At 17 she won four golds at the London 2012 Olympics, and she later swam in college.
Famous swimmers.Adam Peaty: The British breaststroker was the first to swim 100 meters in under 58 seconds, in 2018.
Famous swimmers.Caeleb Dressel: The American sprinter won five golds at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, and five golds at the 2017 world championships.
Famous swimmers.Dara Torres: She competed at five Olympics, and won three medals at age 41 in 2008.
Famous swimmers.Johnny Weissmuller: He won five Olympic golds before starring as Tarzan in the movies, in which his famous yell became legend.
Famous swimmers.Leon Marchand: The French swimmer won four golds at Paris 2024, including sweeping the 200m breaststroke and 200m butterfly.
Famous swimmers.Usain Bolt: The sprinter owns the 100m record of 9.58 and has eight Olympic golds, but swims nowhere.
Famous swimmers.Simone Biles: The gymnast has more world championship medals than anyone, but her sport is gymnastics.
Famous swimmers.Nadia Comaneci: The Romanian gymnast scored the first perfect 10 at the 1976 Olympics, and the scoreboard showed 1.00 because it could not display 10.
Famous swimmers.Carl Lewis: The track star won nine Olympic golds in sprints and long jump, not in pools.
Famous swimmers.Jesse Owens: He won four golds at the 1936 Berlin Olympics in track and field, defying Nazi propaganda.
Famous swimmers.Mo Farah: The British distance runner won double gold in the 5,000m and 10,000m in 2012 and 2016.
Famous swimmers.Shaun White: The snowboarder known as the Flying Tomato is famous for his red hair, and not for swimming.
Famous swimmers.Tony Hawk: The skateboarder landed the first 900 and is not a swimmer.
Famous swimmers.Greg Louganis: The diver is a trap here: diving is a separate sport from swimming, and he famously hit his head on the board in 1988 yet won gold.
Famous swimmers.Tom Daley: The British diver won Olympic gold in 2021 and became known for knitting, but diving is not swimming.
Famous swimmers.Kelly Slater: The surfer won 11 world titles, but surfing is a different sport from swimming.
Famous swimmers.Mary Lou Retton: The American gymnast won the 1984 all-around gold with a perfect 10 on the vault, and is no swimmer.
Famous swimmers.Bode Miller: The American alpine skier won six Olympic medals in snow sports, not swimming pools.

Things from The Legend of Zelda.Link: Link is the hero, not Zelda. Players often mix them up because the series is named for the princess, but Link never speaks in most games.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Zelda: The princess shares her name with Zelda Fitzgerald, wife of F. Scott Fitzgerald, whom Shigeru Miyamoto admired.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Ganon: The villain, whose human form is Ganondorf, is the series' recurring evil king, usually seeking the Triforce.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Hyrule: The kingdom where the games take place; it's been remade over many ages and timelines, which fans love to debate.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Triforce: A sacred relic made of three golden triangles, representing Power, Wisdom and Courage.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Master Sword: The legendary blade that defeats evil. In Ocarina of Time, pulling it from its pedestal sends Link seven years forward in time.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Rupee: Rupees are the gem currency of Hyrule. Their colour shows value, with green worth one and red worth twenty.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Navi: Navi is Link's fairy guide in Ocarina of Time, and her famous 'Hey! Listen!' became a meme.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Epona: Epona is Link's horse. Her name comes from the Celtic goddess of horses.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Hookshot: A grappling tool that lets Link pull himself across gaps by latching on to targets.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Ocarina: In Ocarina of Time, playing songs on it lets Link control time and teleport.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Korok: Small forest spirits hidden around Hyrule in Breath of the Wild, found by solving small puzzles, with 900 seeds to collect.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Deku Tree: The Great Deku Tree is the giant, wise guardian of the Kokiri Forest who gives Link his first quest.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Bowser: Bowser is Mario's rival, king of the Koopas. He's Nintendo but not from Zelda.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Toad: Toad is Mario's mushroom-headed helper, not a Zelda character.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Mushroom Kingdom: The Mushroom Kingdom is the setting of the Mario games, not Hyrule.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Chaos Emerald: Chaos Emeralds are in Sonic the Hedgehog, a Sega series.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Poke Ball: Poke Balls come from Pokemon, not Zelda.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Pikachu: Pikachu is Pokemon's electric mouse, Pokemon's mascot.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Creeper: Creepers are Minecraft's green exploding monsters.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Kirby: Kirby is Nintendo's pink puffball from the Kirby games.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Metroid: Metroid is Nintendo's sci-fi series, with a different heroine, Samus.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Samus: Samus Aran is Metroid's bounty hunter, one of gaming's first female leads.
Things from The Legend of Zelda.Yoshi: Yoshi is Mario's dinosaur friend, not a Zelda character.
