Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Italy: The men have four titles, including in 2006. The Azzurri won back-to-back in 1934 and 1938, and the women haven't won it.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Argentina: Messi finally lifted the trophy in 2022 after a penalty shootout with France, adding to titles from 1978 and 1986.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.France: The men won in 1998 on home soil and again in 2018, with Mbappe scoring in both finals he played in.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Uruguay: The tiny nation won the first World Cup in 1930, hosting it, and again in 1950, beating Brazil at the Maracana.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.England: The men won in 1966 at Wembley and it's their only star, while the women got to the final in 2023, losing to Spain.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Spain: The men's team won in 2010, and in 2023 the women won as well, so Spain holds both trophies.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.USA: The US women have won four titles, the most of any nation, in 1991, 1999, 2015 and 2019, while the men's best was third in 1930.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Norway: The women won the 1995 World Cup, beating Germany in the final, and the men have never won it.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Japan: The women won in 2011, defeating the USA on penalties, and became the first Asian team to win a senior World Cup.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Netherlands: Three men's finals, in 1974, 1978 and 2010, all ended in defeat, and women reached the 2019 final but lost to the USA.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Portugal: Even with Eusebio and Ronaldo, the best finish was third in 1966, and no title exists on the men's side.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Croatia: The men reached the 2018 final, losing to France, and took third in 2022, but the title has eluded them.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Belgium: The men's best was third place in 2018, so their golden generation fell short.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Mexico: El Tri hosted twice, in 1970 and 1986, but never got past the quarterfinals in men's tournaments.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Sweden: The men lost the 1958 final on home soil to Brazil, and the women lost the 2003 final to Germany, so no title.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Hungary: The Magical Magyars lost the 1954 final to West Germany despite being unbeaten for years before, a result called the Miracle of Bern.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Nigeria: The Super Falcons won the Women's Africa Cup many times, but a World Cup title has never come.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Cameroon: In 1990 the Indomitable Lions became the first African team to reach a men's quarterfinal, but they never won.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Chile: The men finished third as hosts in 1962, which is the best finish, and no title has followed.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Colombia: Reaching the quarterfinals in 2014 with James Rodriguez's goals is the men's best result, with no title.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Denmark: The men won Euro 1992 at short notice after Yugoslavia's exclusion, but have never won a World Cup.
Have won the men's or women's FIFA World.Scotland: Despite one of the oldest national teams, Scotland has never advanced past the first round of a men's World Cup.

Cycling terms.Peloton: French for little ball: the main bunch of riders. Tucked inside it, a rider spends far less energy than one pushing into the wind up front.
Cycling terms.Yellow jersey: Worn by the Tour de France leader, it is yellow because sponsor newspaper L'Auto printed on yellow paper. It was first worn in 1919.
Cycling terms.Breakaway: A small group that escapes the peloton. Most breakaways are eventually reeled in, often within sight of the finish, by teams chasing a sprinter.
Cycling terms.Domestique: French for servant: a team rider who fetches bottles, blocks wind for the leader and will even hand over their own bike after a leader's mechanical.
Cycling terms.Time trial: Riders race alone against the clock, with drafting banned, which is why it is nicknamed the race of truth.
Cycling terms.Drafting: Riding in another cyclist's slipstream can save up to about a third of the effort, which is why the peloton exists at all.
Cycling terms.Bonk: Total exhaustion when the body's glycogen runs out. Pros eat constantly during races to avoid it; runners call the same thing hitting the wall.
Cycling terms.Cadence: Pedal revolutions per minute. Pros often spin near 90 rpm, which is gentler on the muscles than grinding a big gear slowly.
Cycling terms.Criterium: A fast race over a short closed loop, often through city streets. Tight corners make it tactical and crash-prone.
Cycling terms.Velodrome: Banked cycling track. Olympic ones are 250 metres around with turns banked at over 40 degrees, and the bikes have no brakes.
Cycling terms.Keirin: Japanese track race created in 1948 for betting. Riders follow a pacing motorbike that peels off before the final sprint; it joined the Olympics in 2000.
Cycling terms.Polka dot jersey: Given to the Tour de France's best climber: white with red dots. It debuted in 1975, reportedly inspired by a chocolate sponsor's wrappers.
Cycling terms.Scrum: A rugby restart where eight forwards per side bind together and shove for the ball. It is rugby's pack, not cycling's.
Cycling terms.Lineout: Rugby restart after the ball goes into touch: teammates lift a jumper skyward to catch the throw. Nothing to do with cycling.
Cycling terms.Wicket: Cricket's target: three stumps topped by two bails. The word also names the pitch strip, so it is no cycling term.
Cycling terms.Googly: A cricket delivery that looks like it will turn one way but spins the other, fooling the batter. Invented in cricket, not cycling.
Cycling terms.Bunker: A sand hazard on a golf course. Sand traps are the opposite of what a peloton wants to ride through.
Cycling terms.Bogey: One stroke over par in golf. The word may come from Colonel Bogey, an imaginary golfer, and has nothing to do with cycling.
Cycling terms.Puck: The hockey disc is vulcanised rubber, about 3 inches wide and frozen before games so it slides rather than bounces.
Cycling terms.Icing: A hockey rule: shooting the puck all the way down the ice from your own half is called icing, a stoppage, not a cycling move.
Cycling terms.Slam dunk: Basketball's flashy dunk. Dunking was banned in the NCAA from 1967 to 1976, largely because of one player, Lew Alcindor.
Cycling terms.Alley-oop: Basketball play where a pass is caught in the air and slammed in. The term comes from French-derived slang 'allez-oop', meaning up.
Cycling terms.Touchdown: American football's scoring play, worth six points. It is football's, not cycling's, though sprint finishes feel similar.
Cycling terms.Checkmate: The chess finish. It comes from Persian shah mat, which is often translated as the king is helpless.

Sega consoles.Genesis: Genesis is the North American name of the Mega Drive, launched in 1989. Its ad campaign famously claimed it did what Nintendon't.
Sega consoles.Master System: The Master System arrived in 1985 as Sega's answer to Nintendo, and did well in Brazil and Europe even as it lagged in Japan and the US.
Sega consoles.Saturn: The Saturn launched in Japan in 1994. It was a hard console to program, and a surprise US launch in 1995 hurt its reputation.
Sega consoles.Dreamcast: Sega's last console, from 1998, was a pioneer of online play with a built-in modem. It was discontinued in 2001.
Sega consoles.Game Gear: Sega's color handheld debuted in 1990 and took on the Game Boy, but it chewed through six AA batteries in a few hours.
Sega consoles.SG-1000: Sega's first home console, released in Japan in 1983. It shared its launch day with Nintendo's Famicom.
Sega consoles.Mega Drive: Mega Drive is the name used for the Genesis in Japan and Europe. Sonic the Hedgehog was its flagship mascot.
Sega consoles.32X: The 32X was an add-on that boosted the Genesis to 32-bit in 1994, and it flopped as the Saturn arrived soon after.
Sega consoles.Sega CD: The Sega CD brought CD-ROM games to the Genesis in 1992, and was known for full-motion video games.
Sega consoles.Nomad: The Nomad was a portable Genesis that played its regular cartridges, released in 1995, but it ate batteries fast.
Sega consoles.Pico: Sega Pico was a 1993 educational console for toddlers, using storybook cartridges. It lasted for years in Japan.
Sega consoles.PlayStation: Sony's PlayStation began as a failed collaboration with Nintendo on a CD add-on. That's why it's Sony's, not Sega's.
Sega consoles.Xbox: Microsoft's Xbox arrived in 2001, built partly from PC parts, so it is not a Sega console.
Sega consoles.GameCube: GameCube is Nintendo's console, from 2001, so it doesn't belong to Sega, despite Sega making games for it.
Sega consoles.Wii: The Wii is Nintendo's motion-controlled console of 2006; Sega developed Sonic games for it, but it isn't theirs.
Sega consoles.Game Boy: Nintendo's handheld, released in 1989. Sega's rival was the Game Gear, not this.
Sega consoles.Atari Jaguar: Atari's 1993 Jaguar was marketed as 64-bit, but it was Atari's, not Sega's, and the console struggled.
Sega consoles.Neo Geo: The Neo Geo is a console by SNK, famed for its arcade-perfect games, and expensive too.
Sega consoles.TurboGrafx-16: NEC's console, sold as the PC Engine in Japan, was a Sega competitor but a different company's.
Sega consoles.3DO: The 3DO was a 1993 console that licensed its hardware to multiple makers, and the machine launched at around $700.
Sega consoles.Virtual Boy: Nintendo's red-tinted 3D headset console of 1995 was a commercial flop, and it isn't Sega's.
Sega consoles.N-Gage: Nokia's N-Gage was a 2003 phone-gaming hybrid, not Sega, and was mocked for needing the battery cover removed to swap games.
Sega consoles.Atari Lynx: Atari's color handheld, from 1989, was ahead of its time with a backlit screen, but it was never Sega's.
Sega consoles.Ouya: Ouya was a 2013 Android microconsole funded through Kickstarter, and it is not a Sega console.

Invented before the year 1500.Wheel: The oldest known wheels, around 3500 BC, were for pottery in Mesopotamia. Wheeled transport came a little later, and the Americas had none for pulling loads.
Invented before the year 1500.Paper: Chinese, dated to about AD 105, and it reached Europe in the 12th century. It replaced costly parchment, which required animal skins.
Invented before the year 1500.Gunpowder: Chinese in origin, from about the 9th century. It reached Europe around the 13th, and soon made castle walls less secure.
Invented before the year 1500.Compass: The Chinese used lodestone for navigation by around the 11th century, and the Europeans were using one by about 1200.
Invented before the year 1500.Printing press: Gutenberg's press of about 1450 was the key tool before 1500. By 1500, over 20 million books had been printed in Europe.
Invented before the year 1500.Eyeglasses: Appeared in Italy in about the 1280s. A monk was said to have praised them in a sermon in 1306 as a recent invention.
Invented before the year 1500.Mechanical clock: Weight-driven clocks with a verge escapement appeared in European towers in the 1300s. They had no faces at first, just bells to ring hours.
Invented before the year 1500.Windmill: Known in Persia and in Europe by the 12th century. They used wind power to grind grain and pump water well before 1500.
Invented before the year 1500.Abacus: A counting frame used since antiquity in various forms, including in Rome and China. It remained in use for centuries.
Invented before the year 1500.Astrolabe: An ancient and medieval instrument for finding stars, and the time. It was used by Islamic astronomers and was an early navigation tool.
Invented before the year 1500.Spinning wheel: Introduced to Europe around the 13th century, perhaps from India. It sped up thread spinning compared to using a hand spindle.
Invented before the year 1500.Crossbow: Used in ancient China and Greece, and widespread in medieval Europe. It could pierce armour.
Invented before the year 1500.Soap: Known to the Babylonians as early as about 2800 BC, who made it from fat and ash. It is much older than 1500.
Invented before the year 1500.Telescope: Patented in 1608 in the Netherlands, so it came after 1500. It transformed astronomy soon afterwards.
Invented before the year 1500.Microscope: Appeared around 1600 and was not widely used until Hooke and Leeuwenhoek in the 17th century.
Invented before the year 1500.Thermometer: Early versions came from Galileo around 1600. Fahrenheit's mercury one came in 1714, so it is post-1500.
Invented before the year 1500.Steam engine: First practical engines came with Newcomen in 1712, which is about 200 years after 1500.
Invented before the year 1500.Pendulum clock: Christiaan Huygens built one in 1656, based on Galileo's insight. It was far more accurate than earlier mechanical clocks.
Invented before the year 1500.Barometer: Evangelista Torricelli made the first one in 1643 using mercury. It followed 1500 by a good while.
Invented before the year 1500.Piano: Cristofori made it in Italy around 1700. It gets its name from its ability to play soft and loud.
Invented before the year 1500.Submarine: Cornelis Drebbel built a rowed one in the early 1600s on the Thames. The first military submarine came later.
Invented before the year 1500.Graphite pencil: Graphite was found in England in 1564, and the wooden pencil spread afterwards. It came shortly after 1500.
Invented before the year 1500.Newspaper: The first regular printed newspapers came in the early 1600s, such as Strasbourg in 1605. The printing press existed earlier, but newspapers followed.
Invented before the year 1500.Light bulb: Late 1800s. Edison and Swan's lamps arrived in 1879 and 1878, hundreds of years after 1500.

Things that fit inside a matchbox.Paper clip: The paper clip is a tiny wire loop whose modern double-oval shape appeared around the late 1800s, and a small matchbox holds dozens.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Coin: A matchbox holds a good handful of coins, which is why matchbox sized treasures are a classic way to hide pocket change.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Button: Buttons are older than you'd think: the earliest known ones, from the Indus Valley, are about 5,000 years old and made of shell.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Thumbtack: The thumbtack was patented in 1900 by Edwin Moore, a Chicago man who simply wanted a better way to pin things to a wall.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Ladybug: Ladybugs make a tiny pet in a matchbox, and their bright red shell warns birds that they taste bitter and are best left alone.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Earring: A single earring fits easily in a matchbox, which is why a tiny box has long been used to smuggle a surprise gift.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Bead: Beads are among the oldest known jewelry: shell beads about 100,000 years old have been found in Africa and the Middle East.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Grain of rice: Some people write on single rice grains: skilled artists can fit a whole poem on one grain with a fine pen.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.SIM card: A modern nano-SIM is just 12.3 by 8.8 mm, so a matchbox could hold hundreds, each one carrying a phone's identity.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Postage stamp: The 1840 Penny Black was the first adhesive postage stamp, and a matchbox easily holds a whole small collection of them.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Ant: Ants can carry up to about 50 times their own weight, so a matchbox of them could in theory shift a lot of cargo.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Safety pin: The safety pin was patented in 1849 by Walter Hunt, who reportedly designed it in three hours to pay off a debt.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Banana: A banana is about 7 inches long and is far too big for a standard matchbox, which is only around 2 inches long.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Smartphone: A smartphone is thin but far too big: matchboxes are about 2 by 1.4 inches, much smaller than even a small phone's face.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Teacup: A teacup is too wide and round to squeeze in, but a dolls' house teacup made for a matchbox would just about fit.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Apple: An apple is about 3 inches across and doesn't come close to fitting; a matchbox holds only a tiny seed of it.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Shoe: A shoe is many times larger than a matchbox, though 'matchbox' toy cars shrunk to fit the size of one are named for it.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Paperback: A paperback is flat, but at around 7 by 4 inches it is several times bigger than the matchbox in every direction.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Hairbrush: A hairbrush is too long, though a folding travel brush does shrink down to about the size of a large matchbox.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.TV remote: A TV remote is about 6 inches long, too big for a matchbox, though the tiny car-key fobs do come near.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Golf ball: A golf ball is 1.68 inches wide by rule, which is almost as wide as the matchbox itself, so it doesn't fit in.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Tennis ball: A tennis ball is about 2.7 inches across, bigger than a standard matchbox in each direction, so it won't fit.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Cupcake: A cupcake is a few inches wide and tall, nowhere near small enough, no matter how mini the bakery makes it.
Things that fit inside a matchbox.Stapler: A desktop stapler is well over 5 inches long, though a mini stapler gets close to matchbox size.

Things a dragon would hoard.Gold coins: Smaug in The Hobbit sleeps on a vast pile of coins, and he notices when a single cup goes missing.
Things a dragon would hoard.Rubies: Rubies are red corundum, harder than almost any gem except diamond, and their fiery color suits a fire-breather.
Things a dragon would hoard.Diamonds: Diamonds are carbon crystals formed deep underground, and they're the hardest natural material known.
Things a dragon would hoard.Crowns: Britain's Imperial State Crown holds over 2,800 diamonds, so a dragon would find the best crowns very rich indeed.
Things a dragon would hoard.Emeralds: Emeralds get their green from chromium, and they're often more fragile than other gems because they're full of tiny flaws.
Things a dragon would hoard.Goblets: In The Hobbit it's a stolen goblet that finally wakes Smaug and sets the story's disaster in motion.
Things a dragon would hoard.Pearls: Pearls are the only gems made by living creatures, built up in layers inside mollusks like oysters.
Things a dragon would hoard.Silver: Silver tarnishes black over time, so a dragon's silver would need polishing, though it conducts electricity better than any other metal.
Things a dragon would hoard.Jewels: Norse legend tells of Fafnir, who turned into a dragon to guard his stolen gold, the model for many later hoards.
Things a dragon would hoard.Sapphires: Sapphires are the same mineral as rubies, corundum, with their blue coming from traces of iron and titanium.
Things a dragon would hoard.Gold bars: A standard gold bar weighs about 12.4 kilograms, or 400 troy ounces, and is dense enough to feel surprisingly heavy.
Things a dragon would hoard.Scepter: The Sovereign's Sceptre in the British Crown Jewels holds the Cullinan I diamond, one of the largest cut diamonds in the world.
Things a dragon would hoard.Socks: Real dragons in legend love shiny things, and socks are the opposite; they just vanish in the wash with no explanation.
Things a dragon would hoard.Broccoli: Broccoli was developed from wild cabbage by Italian farmers, and it's about as unshiny as treasure gets.
Things a dragon would hoard.Rubber duck: In 1992 about 28,800 bath toys, mostly ducks, spilled into the Pacific and drifted across oceans while scientists tracked them.
Things a dragon would hoard.Mop: Hoards are about shine and value, and a mop is neither, which is why no legend has a dragon sleeping on one.
Things a dragon would hoard.Toothbrush: The bristle toothbrush came from China in the 1400s, but no dragon legend wants one.
Things a dragon would hoard.Cabbage: Cabbage is a humble vegetable, and legendary dragons want gleaming things, not something that rots.
Things a dragon would hoard.Spatula: A spatula is a kitchen tool, and it isn't valuable or shiny enough to tempt any self-respecting dragon.
Things a dragon would hoard.Sponge: A natural sponge is actually an animal, among the oldest on Earth, but it's still no dragon treasure.
Things a dragon would hoard.Tissues: Dragon hoards are lasting treasure, and a tissue is made to be thrown away after one use.
Things a dragon would hoard.Teabag: Teabags were reportedly born by accident, when a tea merchant shipped samples in little silk bags around 1908.
Things a dragon would hoard.Carrot: Early carrots were purple or white; orange ones came later, and none of them would tempt a dragon.
Things a dragon would hoard.Shoelace: Even Otzi the iceman, about 5,000 years old, had laced shoes, but a dragon wouldn't want one.

Things an Old West cowboy owns.Lasso: The lasso is a cowboy's rope with a loop, and the word comes from Spanish 'lazo', since American cowboys learned from Mexican vaqueros.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Horse: A cowboy's horse was his partner, and the American West was shaped by the Spanish horses that the Plains tribes came to master.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Saddle: The western saddle has a horn on the front, which cowboys used to anchor a roped steer, and it's far sturdier than English saddles.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Spurs: Spurs have rowels that jingle, and the signature 'jingle bobs' were small pieces added to make a cowboy's spurs ring.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Cowboy hat: The cowboy hat's wide brim shades the sun and sheds rain, and John B. Stetson made the famous 'Boss of the Plains' in 1865.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Boots: Cowboy boots have a tall shaft and slanted heel, designed to grip stirrups and to stop a foot sliding through.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Bandana: A bandana covers the nose and mouth against trail dust, and a damp one cools the neck on a scorching ride.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Harmonica: The harmonica was a cowboy's pocket companion on the trail, small and sturdy enough for nights by the campfire.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Canteen: A canteen holds a cowboy's water on the trail, and a cloth cover that you wet keeps the water cool through evaporation.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Bedroll: A bedroll is the cowboy's bed on the trail, usually a canvas-wrapped set of blankets that doubled as a pillow-rest on the ground.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Chaps: Chaps are leather leg coverings that protect against brush and thorns, and the word comes from the Spanish 'chaparreras'.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Branding iron: A branding iron marks cattle with a ranch's symbol, and brands were registered so an owner could prove his herd.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Horseshoe: A horseshoe protects hooves and is a lucky charm hung above doors, and it's said to be luckiest when the ends point up.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Surfboard: A surfboard fits a beachgoer, and cowboys of the dry plains were rarely near an ocean wave.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Snorkel: A snorkel would have no use on dusty cattle drives, and the first snorkels were used by ancient divers with hollow reeds.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Laptop: A laptop would have been a century-plus off for any cowboy, and the first portable computers came in the 1980s.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Ballet slippers: Ballet slippers are for dancers, and in the Old West the nearest thing to dance shoes were boots at a saloon hoedown.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Skis: Skis belong to snowy slopes, not the cattle trail, though the Old West's high mountains did have miners using snowshoes.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Space helmet: A space helmet is a century off, and the first human reached orbit in 1961, long after the cowboy era ended.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Smartwatch: A smartwatch is modern, and a cowboy checked the time with a pocket watch if he had one.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Scuba fins: Scuba fins are for diving, and the aqualung that made scuba possible was invented in the 1940s.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Toga: A toga is what ancient Romans wore, and cowboys favored denim and leather over robes.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Jet ski: A jet ski needs an engine and a lake, and the first one came from the 1960s, far after the Old West.
Things an Old West cowboy owns.Hoverboard: A hoverboard is from science fiction, and cowboys would have thought it witchcraft.

Things you can ride.Horse: Horses can sleep standing up thanks to a locking mechanism in their legs, but they lie down for deep sleep.
Things you can ride.Bicycle: The 1880s 'safety bicycle', with two equal wheels and a chain drive, made cycling practical and popular, even for women's independence.
Things you can ride.Roller coaster: Roller coasters grew from Russian ice slides of the 1600s; the first American ones opened at Coney Island in the 1880s.
Things you can ride.Camel: A camel's hump stores fat, not water; one can drink over 100 litres in minutes after a long trek.
Things you can ride.Wave: Surfers ride waves that began as wind energy far out at sea, sometimes travelling thousands of kilometres before they break.
Things you can ride.Skateboard: Skateboards were invented in 1950s California by surfers who wanted something to ride when the waves were flat.
Things you can ride.Bus: The red double-decker is iconic in London, but the word 'bus' comes from Latin omnibus, meaning 'for all'.
Things you can ride.Elephant: Elephants have been ridden in Asia for thousands of years; their feet sweat through their toenails, and they can swim.
Things you can ride.Escalator: Escalators were first shown at the 1900 Paris Exposition; 'escalator' was originally a trademark of Otis.
Things you can ride.Zip line: Some of the longest zip lines let riders top 100 km/h, and Wales has one that runs over a flooded quarry.
Things you can ride.Donkey: Donkeys have been used as mounts for 5,000 years; they're famous for stubbornness, which is really a strong sense of caution.
Things you can ride.Ferris wheel: The first Ferris wheel, built for the 1893 Chicago fair, stood about 80 metres tall and carried 2,000 riders at once.
Things you can ride.Cloud: A trap: a cloud can't be ridden, though Chinese legend gave Sun Wukong a magic cloud to ride.
Things you can ride.Rainbow: You can't ride a rainbow; it's an optical effect with no location, and it moves as you do.
Things you can ride.Goldfish: Goldfish can be kept as pets but are far too small to ride; they can live for decades in good care.
Things you can ride.Butterfly: Butterflies weigh less than a gram, so nothing rideable here; the monarch migrates thousands of kilometres.
Things you can ride.Snail: Snails move at about 1 mm per second, and while children sometimes race them, nobody rides one.
Things you can ride.Cactus: A cactus is a prickly plant and certainly no steed; many store water in their stems for dry spells.
Things you can ride.Jellyfish: Jellyfish are about 95 percent water, have no brain, and are not rideable, though some live on the ocean's drifting current.
Things you can ride.Hamster: Hamsters are tiny; they can stuff food in cheek pouches and run several kilometres on a wheel in a night.
Things you can ride.Pigeon: Pigeons can carry messages but not riders; they navigate partly by Earth's magnetic field.
Things you can ride.Lobster: Lobsters crawl along the seabed and nobody rides one; their blood is clear but turns blue when it meets oxygen.
Things you can ride.Ladybug: Ladybugs can't carry a rider; a single ladybug may eat up to 5,000 aphids in its lifetime.
Things you can ride.Moth: Moths are mostly night fliers, and while some lack mouths as adults, none can carry a rider.

Things that would make a useless umbrell.Colander: A colander has holes designed to let water out, so rain would drip straight through onto you.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Sieve: A sieve is a mesh made for draining; as an umbrella it lets the whole rainstorm filter through.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Tennis racket: The strings and gaps of a tennis racket let rain pass through, so you'd be soaked despite holding it overhead.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Fishing net: A fishing net is made of holes, and an umbrella needs a continuous surface; it would catch fish, not rain.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Hula hoop: A hula hoop is only a ring with nothing stretched across it, so rain falls through the middle.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Lace doily: A lace doily is all delicate open patterns, so it gives fashion but no shelter from the rain.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Screen door: A screen door's mesh keeps bugs out but lets raindrops straight through.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Swiss cheese: Real Swiss cheese has holes, called eyes, formed by bubbles of gas from bacteria; as a canopy it leaks.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Picture frame: A picture frame has an empty centre, so your head would get wet in the frame's opening.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Chain-link fence: A chain-link fence is a grid of gaps, and the rain just falls through every diamond.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Trash bag: A trap: a trash bag is waterproof and makes a decent emergency rain cover, so it works as an umbrella.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Tarp: A tarp is a waterproof sheet, which is why hikers use it as a shelter; it would work well overhead.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Pizza box: A pizza box is cardboard that holds up in light rain for a while, so it's a passable temporary cover.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Baking tray: A baking tray is solid metal, so it would keep rain off, though it would make clanging noises.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Frying pan: A frying pan is solid and wide enough to shield your head, so it would actually keep the rain off.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Shower curtain: A shower curtain is made of waterproof plastic, so it would work as an umbrella if you could hold it up.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Large leaf: People in the tropics have long used large leaves, like banana leaves, as natural umbrellas; they work.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Beach umbrella: A beach umbrella is a trap of sorts: it's built for sun, but its canopy keeps rain off just fine.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Cardboard box: A cardboard box on your head would shield you for a short while before it gets soggy and collapses.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Trash can lid: A trash can lid is solid and round, so you could hold it overhead as a classic makeshift shield.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Hard hat: A hard hat is made to shed falling objects, and rain slides off it; it's more of a hat than an umbrella.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Surfboard: A surfboard is a waterproof, solid surface, and held overhead it would shield you from rain quite well.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Rubber raft: A rubber raft is made to be waterproof, so held up it keeps rain off, though it's awkward to carry.
Things that would make a useless umbrell.Cutting board: A cutting board is solid, flat and wide enough to cover your head, so it works despite looking silly.

Products that come from sheep.Wool: Sheep wool is a renewable fibre that keeps warm even when damp. A single sheep may produce several pounds of fleece in a year.
Products that come from sheep.Lanolin: A waxy grease from sheep's wool, which waterproofs the fleece. It's used in lip balms, skin creams and some ointments.
Products that come from sheep.Mutton: Meat from mature sheep, with a stronger flavor than lamb. It was once far more popular in Britain than it is now.
Products that come from sheep.Lamb chops: Cut from young sheep. Spring lamb is traditional at Easter in many cultures.
Products that come from sheep.Sheepskin: Used in rugs and boots, sheepskin keeps heat in. Ugg boots are a famous example of this material.
Products that come from sheep.Feta: This Greek cheese is protected by EU rules: only feta made in Greece from sheep's milk, or a mix with goat milk, can use the name.
Products that come from sheep.Roquefort: A French blue cheese made from ewe's milk and ripened in caves. Its blue veins come from a mould called Penicillium roqueforti.
Products that come from sheep.Pecorino: Italian cheeses made from sheep's milk. 'Pecora' means sheep in Italian, and pecorino romano is an ancient Roman favorite.
Products that come from sheep.Haggis: A Scottish dish of sheep's offal, oatmeal and spices, traditionally boiled in a stomach. It's honored every January on Burns Night.
Products that come from sheep.Silk: Spun by silkworm caterpillars, not mammals. Silk fibre can reach up to a mile in a single cocoon thread.
Products that come from sheep.Cashmere: Comes from the fine undercoat of cashmere goats. It's softer and warmer than sheep's wool, so it costs more.
Products that come from sheep.Mohair: The shiny fibre from Angora goats, not sheep. Don't confuse them with Angora rabbits.
Products that come from sheep.Angora: Fluffy fibre from Angora rabbits, though 'Angora' also names a goat breed. Both fibres aren't sheep wool.
Products that come from sheep.Alpaca wool: From alpacas, which are camel relatives from South America. It lacks wool's lanolin, so some people find it less itchy.
Products that come from sheep.Cheddar: A cow's milk cheese from the English village of Cheddar. It's traditionally aged in cool caves.
Products that come from sheep.Mozzarella: Traditionally made from water buffalo milk in southern Italy. The cheaper cow's milk version is more common worldwide.
Products that come from sheep.Honey: Bees make honey by repeatedly regurgitating nectar. Sealed honey from ancient Egyptian tombs has been found still edible.
Products that come from sheep.Eggs: Eggs come from hens. The shell has thousands of tiny pores, allowing air to pass through.
Products that come from sheep.Bacon: Cured pork belly. The phrase 'bring home the bacon' may come from an old English contest.
Products that come from sheep.Beef: Cattle meat. The word comes from Old French, while 'cow' is Anglo-Saxon, a legacy of the Norman conquest.
Products that come from sheep.Brie: A soft cow's milk cheese from France, whose bloomy white rind is edible. Not sheep.
Products that come from sheep.Gouda: A Dutch cow's milk cheese named after the town of Gouda, though it's usually pronounced 'HOW-da'.
Products that come from sheep.Down feathers: Soft feathers from ducks and geese, used in jackets and bedding. Birds, not sheep.
Products that come from sheep.Parmesan: Parmigiano-Reggiano is made from cow's milk. Its wheels are aged for at least a year.

Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Chemist: Chemist starts with Ch. In Britain, it's also the everyday word for the pharmacy on the high street.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Chauffeur: Chauffeur comes from the French word for 'stoker', because early steam cars needed someone to feed the fire.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Chiropractor: Chiropractic was founded in 1895 by D. D. Palmer in Iowa, and its name comes from Greek for 'done by hand'.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Choreographer: A choreographer designs dance movements, and the word comes from Greek for 'dance writing'.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Chimney sweep: In Britain, meeting a chimney sweep is considered good luck, and sweeps are often hired for weddings.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Chaplain: A chaplain serves in a hospital, the military or prison, and the word comes from the 'chapel' of St. Martin's cloak.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Chancellor: Chancellor comes from Latin 'cancellarius', a doorkeeper at a lattice screen. Today it's also Germany's head of government.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Chairman: Chairman is the person who presides over a meeting or a company's board, and the word is now often replaced by 'chair'.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Cheesemaker: Cheesemakers turn milk into cheese using cultures and rennet, and some aged cheeses take years to mature.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Choirmaster: A choirmaster trains and conducts a choir, a job with centuries of church tradition behind it.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Chandler: A chandler originally made candles, and today a ship chandler sells supplies for boats, so it starts with Ch and fits.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Cashier: Cashier starts with 'Ca', not 'Ch', so it's out despite the similar sound at the start of the word.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Carpenter: Carpenter starts with 'Ca', and comes from the Latin 'carpentarius', a maker of carts, so it doesn't start with Ch.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Coach: Coach starts with 'Co'. The word comes from Kocs, a Hungarian town known for its carriages, so it's out.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Courier: Courier starts with 'Co', so it doesn't start with Ch. A courier delivers packages or messages.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Cook: Cook starts with a hard C, and though it's close in meaning to chef, it doesn't start with Ch.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Clerk: Clerk starts with 'Cl', and the word comes from 'cleric', because early clerks were churchmen.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Cobbler: A cobbler repairs shoes, and also names a fruit dessert, but it starts with 'Co', not 'Ch'.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Caddie: A caddie carries a golfer's clubs, and the word comes from the French 'cadet', or young boy.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Cleaner: A cleaner starts with 'Cl', not 'Ch', so it's out, however much it might sound like a Ch job.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Curator: A curator manages a museum's collection, and starts with 'Cu', not 'Ch', so it doesn't fit this list.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Conductor: A conductor leads an orchestra, and starts with 'Co', not 'Ch', so it doesn't count for this list.
Jobs that start with 'Ch'.Cartographer: A cartographer makes maps, and starts with 'Ca', not 'Ch', so it doesn't fit this list of jobs.

Companies that have made mobile phones.Apple: Apple's first iPhone arrived in 2007 with no app store and no copy-paste. Steve Jobs pitched it as a widescreen iPod, a phone and an internet device in one.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Samsung: Samsung started in 1938 as a Korean trading company dealing in dried fish and noodles. It is now one of the world's largest phone makers.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Google: Google bought Motorola's phone arm in 2012, sold it to Lenovo, and later launched its own Pixel phones in 2016.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Motorola: A Motorola engineer, Martin Cooper, made the first public handheld cell phone call in 1973. The 1983 DynaTAC weighed almost a kilogram and cost nearly $4,000.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Nokia: Nokia began as a Finnish paper mill in the 1860s. Its 1100 phone, from 2003, is believed to be among the best-selling consumer electronics devices ever.
Companies that have made mobile phones.OnePlus: OnePlus, founded in 2013, built early buzz with an invite-only sales system and the slogan "Never Settle." It grew quickly with flagship-level phones at lower prices.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Xiaomi: Xiaomi, founded in 2010, became one of the world's top phone sellers within about a decade. Its name is often translated as "millet," though the origin story varies.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Huawei: Chinese company Huawei was founded in 1987 and grew from telecom equipment into one of the world's largest phone makers. Its name loosely means "splendid achievement."
Companies that have made mobile phones.Sony: Sony teamed up with Ericsson in 2001 to make phones, and later bought out its partner's share. Its Xperia line has run since 2008.
Companies that have made mobile phones.LG: LG's name started as Lucky Goldstar. In 2021 the company announced it would exit the phone business after years of falling sales.
Companies that have made mobile phones.BlackBerry: BlackBerry phones with physical keyboards became so addictive that people jokingly called them "CrackBerries." Their popularity faded after the iPhone arrived.
Companies that have made mobile phones.HTC: HTC built the first Android phone, the T-Mobile G1, in 2008. The Taiwanese firm once made phones under other companies' brand names.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Ericsson: Sweden's Ericsson was once a major phone maker, and Sony Ericsson later made Walkman and Cyber-shot phones together. Today it focuses mainly on network equipment.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Netflix: Netflix started in 1997 by mailing DVDs to customers, and it moved into streaming in 2007. It makes apps that run on phones, not the phones themselves.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Spotify: Spotify, founded in Sweden in 2006, made its name streaming music. It builds an app for phones, not hardware, though it did sell a car-based gadget.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Uber: Uber began in 2009 as a way to hail a black car from your phone. It depends on smartphones but has never built one.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Twitter: Twitter, started in 2006, limited posts to 140 characters, a nod to SMS text limits. It's an app on phones, not a phone maker.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Adobe: Adobe makes software such as Photoshop and the PDF format. Its apps run on phones, but it has never made handsets.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Oracle: Oracle is known for databases and enterprise software, founded in 1977. It owns Java, which ran on billions of phones, but it doesn't build phones.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Nintendo: Nintendo started in 1889 as a playing-card company. It makes handheld game consoles, not mobile phones, though its games now appear on them.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Canon: Canon makes cameras and printers, and is a major name in imaging. Its cameras influenced phone photography, but it doesn't sell phones.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Dropbox: Dropbox began in 2007 as a cloud file-storage tool, reportedly after founder Drew Houston forgot his USB drive on a bus. It's an app, not a handset.
Companies that have made mobile phones.eBay: eBay started in 1995 as an auction site, and its first sale was reportedly a broken laser pointer. Lots of phones sell there, but it doesn't make them.
Companies that have made mobile phones.Zoom: Zoom video calling exploded during the 2020 pandemic, growing from 10 million to 300 million daily meeting participants. It's software that runs on phones.

Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Google Assistant: It debuted in 2016 and could place a restaurant call for you with a human-sounding voice in a 2018 Duplex demo.

Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Grok: Made by xAI, it takes its name from a Robert Heinlein novel, where 'to grok' means to understand something deeply.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Roomba: A vacuum robot made by iRobot. It navigates and cleans on its own, but it isn't a conversational assistant.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Fitbit: Fitbit made step-counting wristbands and was bought by Google. It tracks activity rather than chatting back.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Kindle: Amazon's e-reader uses e-ink that looks like paper. It's a reading device, not a voice assistant or chatbot.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Tamagotchi: This 1996 Japanese virtual pet beeps for attention, but its handful of pixels doesn't make it a chatbot.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Furby: The 1998 toy seems to learn English over time, but it was scripted to reveal built-in words gradually, not to converse.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Zune: Microsoft's iPod rival of 2006 was a music player, not an assistant, and it was discontinued in 2012.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Pixel: Google's Pixel phones are hardware that run Google Assistant, which is the actual assistant in this group.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Firefox: A browser from Mozilla. It has no assistant of its own, though people now use chatbots inside it.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Spotify: A streaming service with recommendation algorithms, but it's a music app rather than a conversational chatbot.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Shazam: It names songs by matching a short audio fingerprint, which is clever listening but not a conversation. Apple bought it in 2018.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Waze: This navigation app crowdsources traffic reports from drivers; Google bought it in 2013 and it isn't a chatbot.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Tinder: The dating app is built on swiping profiles, not on chatting with an AI.
Voice assistants and AI chatbots.Excel: Excel is a spreadsheet program; it has formulas and now AI features, but it isn't a voice assistant or chatbot.

Text formatting styles.Bold: Heavier type became popular in the 1800s for posters and ads; today it's usually a Ctrl+B away.
Text formatting styles.Italic: Named for Italy; Aldus Manutius introduced it around 1500 to fit more text on a page.
Text formatting styles.Underline: Typewriters made underlines by backspacing, and on the web underlining is now mostly reserved for links.
Text formatting styles.Strikethrough: Used in legal drafts and edits to show text that has been deleted but is still readable.
Text formatting styles.Superscript: Raised text, used for exponents and for ordinal endings like 1st.
Text formatting styles.Subscript: Lowered text, as in H2O, used heavily in chemistry and math.
Text formatting styles.Highlight: It mimics highlighter pens, which were popularized by the Hi-Liter in 1963.
Text formatting styles.All caps: Online it is read as shouting, but lawyers and designers use it for emphasis.
Text formatting styles.Small caps: Capital-shaped letters at lowercase height; typographers use them for acronyms so they don't shout.
Text formatting styles.Spell check: A tool, not a style; the first spell checker appeared at Stanford in 1971.
Text formatting styles.Word count: A tool that counts words, not a style that changes how the text looks.
Text formatting styles.Save as: A command to save a file under a new name, not a text style.
Text formatting styles.Print preview: A view option that shows how a page will look on paper, not a formatting style.
Text formatting styles.Undo: Usually Ctrl+Z; it reverses your last action rather than styling text.
Text formatting styles.Autosave: A feature that saves your work automatically, not a style that changes how text looks.
Text formatting styles.Track changes: A tricky one: it shows edits with color and strikethrough, but it's a review feature, not a style.
Text formatting styles.Zoom: Zooming changes only how big the page looks on screen, not the text itself.
Text formatting styles.Copy: Larry Tesler invented cut, copy and paste at Xerox PARC, but copying isn't a style.
Text formatting styles.Paste: A command that inserts clipboard contents rather than a text style.
Text formatting styles.Find: A command to search for text, not to change how it looks.
Text formatting styles.Thesaurus: A reference tool for synonyms; it doesn't change how text looks.
Text formatting styles.Mail merge: A feature that fills a template letter from a list of names and addresses, not formatting.
Text formatting styles.Page count: A page count only tells you the document length and doesn't change how any text looks.
Text formatting styles.Search: A search function that locates text, not a formatting style.
