Archive file extensions..zip: Short for Zip, created by Phil Katz in 1989, which is the archive format most people have used at some point.
Archive file extensions..rar: The Roshal Archive, invented by Eugene Roshal, often compresses better than zip, but making .rar files needs WinRAR software.
Archive file extensions..7z: 7-Zip's format often compresses better than zip, and the free open-source tool is widely used.
Archive file extensions..tar: Short for tape archive, it bundles files without shrinking them, so it's typically paired with gzip or xz.
Archive file extensions..gz: Gzip compresses a single file, which is why Linux archives are commonly .tar.gz, bundled then compressed.
Archive file extensions..bz2: Bzip2 often compresses smaller than gzip, though more slowly, and is common in older Unix software.
Archive file extensions..tgz: A shorthand for .tar.gz, a bundle of files compressed with gzip, created so it fits old 8.3 filename limits.
Archive file extensions..xz: A format based on LZMA that gives very small files and is used by many Linux distributions to ship software.
Archive file extensions..cab: Microsoft's cabinet format, used in Windows installers and updates, and holds multiple compressed files.
Archive file extensions..exe: A program file, not an archive, though some installers are self-extracting archives wrapped in an executable.
Archive file extensions..pdf: An Adobe document format, not an archive, though it can embed attachments and compresses its own contents.
Archive file extensions..jpg: JPEG photos are already compressed, which is why zipping them barely saves space, and not an archive.
Archive file extensions..mp3: MP3 is already compressed audio, which is why zipping it barely shrinks it, and not an archive.
Archive file extensions..ppt: The old binary PowerPoint format, not an archive. The newer .pptx format is secretly a zip file, though.
Archive file extensions..txt: Plain text compresses wonderfully, so it is among the best things to put in an archive, but it isn't one.
Archive file extensions..png: PNG already uses lossless compression internally, so zipping barely shrinks it, and it isn't an archive.
Archive file extensions..html: A web page file made of markup, which is easy to compress but not itself an archive.
Archive file extensions..css: A stylesheet file for web pages, and plain text, which compresses well but isn't an archive.
Archive file extensions..js: A JavaScript source file; minified versions shrink it further, but it's code, not an archive.
Archive file extensions..py: A Python script file, plain text that doesn't bundle other files, so it's not an archive.
Archive file extensions..csv: Comma-separated values are plain-text tables that zip down tiny, but a CSV isn't an archive.
Archive file extensions..mov: Apple's QuickTime video container, which holds video and audio, not a bundle of files.
Archive file extensions..wav: Uncompressed audio from Microsoft and IBM; it shrinks a lot when zipped, but it isn't an archive.
Archive file extensions..psd: Photoshop's layered image file, often huge, which compresses internally; an image document, not an archive.

Email services.Gmail: Launched on April 1, 2004, with a then-huge 1 GB of storage, which many people assumed was an April Fools' joke.
Email services.Outlook: Microsoft's mail service took over from Hotmail in 2013, and its name also lives on in the Outlook desktop app in Office.
Email services.Yahoo Mail: One of the oldest webmail services, launched in 1997; a breach disclosed in 2017 turned out to have hit all 3 billion accounts.
Email services.Hotmail: Founded in 1996 and sold to Microsoft in 1997, its original name capitalized 'HoTMaiL' as a nod to the HTML language.
Email services.AOL Mail: AOL's old 'You've got mail!' greeting was a real voice recording by Elwood Edwards, and became a pop-culture catchphrase.
Email services.Proton Mail: Created at the CERN research lab in Switzerland in 2014, it encrypts messages end to end, so even the company can't read them.
Email services.iCloud Mail: Apple's @icloud.com addresses sit beside older @me.com and @mac.com ones, relics of Apple's earlier online services.
Email services.Zoho Mail: Zoho is an Indian software company, founded in Chennai, that runs ad-free business email alongside a giant suite of office apps.
Email services.GMX: A German provider whose name stands for 'Global Mail eXchange'; it started in 1997 and is a household name for email in Germany.
Email services.Yandex Mail: From Russia's biggest search company, whose name Yandex is said to mean 'Yet Another iNDEXer'.
Email services.Fastmail: An Australian email service founded in 1999, known for charging a fee instead of showing ads, and for pushing the open JMAP protocol.
Email services.Slack: Slack began inside a game company whose game failed; its name is said to stand for 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'. Chat, not email.
Email services.WhatsApp: Facebook bought it in 2014 for around 19 billion dollars, yet it works through phone numbers and has no email inbox at all.
Email services.Telegram: Founded by the Russian brothers Pavel and Nikolai Durov, it is a messaging app tied to phone numbers, not an email service.
Email services.Discord: Launched in 2015 for gamers, it uses usernames and servers for chat; you sign up with an email address but get no inbox.
Email services.Signal: Its encryption protocol is so well regarded that WhatsApp adopted it too; the app itself is chat, not email.
Email services.Zoom: Its use leapt from about 10 million daily meeting participants in late 2019 to roughly 300 million by April 2020. It's video, not email.
Email services.Skype: Founded in 2003 with Estonian engineers behind it, bought by Microsoft in 2011 for 8.5 billion dollars; it is a calling app, not email.
Email services.Teams: Microsoft's workplace chat arrived in 2017 and comes bundled with Outlook in Microsoft 365, but it is chat rather than email.
Email services.WeChat: Tencent's super-app has over a billion users and bundles chat, payments and mini programs, but no email inboxes.
Email services.Viber: Founded in Israel in 2010 and later bought by Japan's Rakuten, it is a calling and messaging app rather than an email service.
Email services.Messenger: Facebook once offered @facebook.com email addresses, but the Messenger app itself is only for chat.
Email services.Snapchat: Pioneered disappearing photos and stories; it's a photo-messaging app with usernames, not an email service.
Email services.Kik: A Canadian chat app launched in 2010 that let people sign up with a username rather than a phone number; it has no email inbox.

Characters in The Tempest.Prospero: The exiled Duke of Milan rules the island with the help of his magic books, which he plans to drown.
Characters in The Tempest.Miranda: Raised on the island, she has seen almost no men besides her father, and her first sight of Ferdinand charms her.
Characters in The Tempest.Ariel: The spirit serves Prospero in exchange for his freedom and delivers some of the play's loveliest songs.
Characters in The Tempest.Caliban: The island's native was enslaved by Prospero, and his name may be an anagram of the word 'cannibal'.
Characters in The Tempest.Ferdinand: The prince of Naples falls in love with Miranda and is given logs to carry as a test.
Characters in The Tempest.Alonso: The King of Naples believes his son has drowned, and he grieves in the shipwreck's aftermath.
Characters in The Tempest.Antonio: Prospero's treacherous brother, who took his dukedom, is eventually forced to confront his crime.
Characters in The Tempest.Gonzalo: The kindly old counsellor who secretly aided Prospero's escape sets out his vision of an ideal commonwealth.
Characters in The Tempest.Trinculo: The jester gets drunk with Caliban and plots to murder Prospero, a subplot of pure slapstick.
Characters in The Tempest.Stephano: The drunken butler becomes Caliban's would-be master and plots with him to kill Prospero.
Characters in The Tempest.Sebastian: He is Alonso's brother who plots to kill the king, but also the name of the twin in Twelfth Night.
Characters in The Tempest.Puck: The mischievous fairy belongs to A Midsummer Night's Dream, not to Prospero's island.
Characters in The Tempest.Oberon: The fairy king belongs to A Midsummer Night's Dream, a very different magic from Prospero's.
Characters in The Tempest.Viola: The shipwrecked heroine of Twelfth Night, not Prospero's island.
Characters in The Tempest.Olivia: The countess in Twelfth Night, who falls for Viola in disguise.
Characters in The Tempest.Malvolio: The pompous steward of Twelfth Night, whose yellow stockings made him a laughing stock.
Characters in The Tempest.Iago: The scheming villain of Othello, not a resident of Prospero's island.
Characters in The Tempest.Hamlet: The Danish prince from a tragedy, not the Tempest.
Characters in The Tempest.King Lear: The aging king divides his kingdom among his daughters in his own tragedy.
Characters in The Tempest.Portia: The clever heroine of The Merchant of Venice, in the courtroom.
Characters in The Tempest.Benedick: The witty lover in Much Ado About Nothing, who sparred with Beatrice.
Characters in The Tempest.Beatrice: His sparring partner in Much Ado About Nothing is known for her quick wit.
Characters in The Tempest.Juliet: The heroine of Romeo and Juliet, from a very different play.
Characters in The Tempest.Perdita: The lost daughter in The Winter's Tale, from a romance with its own bear.

Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Potions: Snape's dungeon class involves precise brewing; in Harry's first year it nearly always begins with Snape picking on him.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Transfiguration: McGonagall's class turns matches into needles and, later, animals into goblets; she herself is an Animagus who becomes a cat.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Charms: Tiny Professor Flitwick teaches this spell class, home to Wingardium Leviosa; it's the 'leviOsa, not levioSA' lesson.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Herbology: Professor Sprout's greenhouse class covers magical plants like Mandrake, whose cry can knock students out.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Divination: Professor Trelawney's class of reading tea leaves and crystal balls is dismissed by McGonagall as imprecise.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Astronomy: Studied at night with telescopes in a tower, this is real science that Hogwarts students chart, with Professor Sinistra teaching.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Arithmancy: A magical branch of numerology, taken by Hermione from third year; it's the real name of divination by numbers.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.History of Magic: Taught by the ghost Professor Binns, who famously didn't notice he'd died and kept teaching.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Muggle Studies: Taught by Charity Burbage, it studies non-magical people's lives; Hermione took it, and Voldemort later killed its teacher.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Ancient Runes: Students translate ancient symbols in this class, which Hermione takes; real runes were used by early Germanic peoples.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Flying: Madam Hooch teaches first-years on broomsticks, and Harry's first lesson ends with his chasing Neville's Remembrall.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Quidditch: It's played at Hogwarts but not taught; Madam Hooch referees the matches, and no one studies it for a grade.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Chemistry: A real science, but not on Hogwarts's timetable; potions covers what chemistry does at a magical school.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Latin: Though spells sound Latin-like, it isn't a Hogwarts subject; the incantations just borrow from it.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Algebra: Not taught at Hogwarts; the school's maths-and-magic subject is Arithmancy instead.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Sorcery: Not a Hogwarts subject: the spell-teaching subject is called Charms, and sorcery isn't on offer.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Necromancy: Magic dealing with the dead isn't taught at Hogwarts, where Defence Against the Dark Arts is the nearest subject.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Geography: No geography on the Hogwarts timetable; students learn about the wizarding world through other classes.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Physics: Not at Hogwarts; magic does the work that real physics explains elsewhere.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Biology: Biology isn't a subject at Hogwarts; Care of Magical Creatures covers beasts like hippogriffs.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Music: Hogwarts has a choir and a frog choir, but no music class on the official schedule.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Drama: No drama class at Hogwarts, though students stage a Christmas ball every Triwizard year.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Woodwork: Not on the curriculum; wand-making is a trade done by shops like Ollivanders.
Subjects taught at Hogwarts.Botany: A real-world subject for plants, but Hogwarts calls its plant class Herbology.

Theater terms.Proscenium: Greek for 'before the scene': the arch that frames a stage like a picture frame, separating audience from action.
Theater terms.Wings: The unseen side areas offstage, where actors wait for their cues; the term dates back to when painted flats hid them.
Theater terms.Curtain call: Cast members bow in order, with the stars usually last; the ritual of the bow dates back centuries.
Theater terms.Understudy: Learns a role to step in if the lead is out; a 'swing' covers several roles in the ensemble.
Theater terms.Stage left: Directions are from the actor's view facing the audience, so stage left is the audience's right.
Theater terms.Upstage: The back of the stage, once literally raised on a slope; to 'upstage' someone is to steal their scene.
Theater terms.Intermission: A break between acts, called an interval in Britain, that gives theaters a chance to sell snacks and drinks.
Theater terms.Matinee: From the French for 'morning', though these shows are in the afternoon; the name stuck when performances moved later.
Theater terms.Soliloquy: A speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud alone; Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' is the most famous.
Theater terms.Blocking: The director's plan for where and when actors move; some say it comes from plotting moves with wooden blocks on a model stage.
Theater terms.Footlights: The row of lights along the stage's front edge were originally candles or gas lamps, whose upward glow gave faces an eerie look.
Theater terms.Green room: The backstage lounge where actors wait; no one is sure why it is called green, and most are not green at all.
Theater terms.Dress rehearsal: The final full run-through in costume with lights and sound, usually a day or so before opening night.
Theater terms.Crescendo: A musical term for getting gradually louder, from the Italian for 'growing', not a theater word.
Theater terms.Allegro: A tempo marking meaning brisk and lively, from the Italian for 'cheerful'; it belongs to music.
Theater terms.Staccato: A music term for short, sharp, detached notes, from the Italian for 'detached'; the opposite of legato.
Theater terms.Sfumato: A painting technique of soft, smoky blending; Leonardo used it on the Mona Lisa's smile.
Theater terms.Chiaroscuro: A painting term for strong light-dark contrast, Italian for 'light-dark'; Caravaggio and Rembrandt mastered it.
Theater terms.Fresco: A painting technique on wet plaster, from the Italian for 'fresh'; Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling is the most famous example.
Theater terms.Stanza: A group of lines in a poem, from the Italian for 'room', since each stanza is a small room in the poem.
Theater terms.Byline: The line naming a news story's author, a journalism term; the name is a stage far from theater, though it has a 'line' like scripts.
Theater terms.Offside: A football (soccer) rule that stops attackers from lurking beside the goal; it is often debated and now checked by video review.
Theater terms.Touchdown: American football's six-point score, though the ball does not need to touch the ground.
Theater terms.Shutter: A camera part controlling exposure time; fast ones can open for less than a thousandth of a second.

Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Scout: Jean Louise Finch narrates the book as an adult remembering her childhood, and is a tomboy who prefers fights to dresses.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Atticus Finch: Harper Lee's lawyer hero defends a Black man falsely accused of rape and tells his daughter you never understand someone until you walk in their skin.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Jem: Scout's older brother breaks his arm protecting her from Bob Ewell's attack and grows up fast across the story.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Boo Radley: The mysterious neighbour who leaves gifts in a tree hollow turns out to be a gentle protector, and the town's real mockingbird.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Dill: The visiting boy who loves stories was modelled on Lee's real childhood friend Truman Capote.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Calpurnia: The Finch family's Black housekeeper raises the children firmly and takes them to her church, widening Scout's world.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Tom Robinson: The Black field hand falsely accused of rape is convicted by an all-white jury despite his innocence, and is later shot trying to escape prison.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Bob Ewell: The vicious, poor white father who accuses Tom lies in court and later attacks Atticus's children.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Mayella Ewell: The lonely young woman accuses Tom Robinson, and is a pitiable figure trapped by her violent father's lie.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Miss Maudie: The neighbour who bakes cakes and gardens fiercely is one of Scout's few female role models and Atticus's friend.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Heck Tate: The sheriff decides to protect Boo Radley by saying Bob Ewell fell on his own knife, an arguable act of justice.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Holden Caulfield: Salinger's teen narrator loathes "phonies" in New York, far from Maycomb, Alabama.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Huck Finn: Twain's raft-riding runaway only shares a near-name with Atticus Finch; he belongs to the Mississippi, not Maycomb.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Lennie Small: Steinbeck's strong, simple-minded ranch hand is from Of Mice and Men, set in California.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Jay Gatsby: Fitzgerald's mysterious millionaire belongs to the Jazz Age, not 1930s Alabama.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Nick Carraway: The narrator of The Great Gatsby is a Long Island bond salesman, not a Maycomb local.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Ponyboy Curtis: The greaser narrator of The Outsiders was created by S. E. Hinton, who wrote it as a teenager.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Hester Prynne: Hawthorne's scarlet-letter heroine lives in Puritan Boston, not 1930s Alabama.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Ishmael: The narrator of Moby-Dick sails from Massachusetts, not from a small Alabama town.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Jo March: Another famous young tomboy, but from Little Women, set around the Civil War in New England.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Scarlett O'Hara: Margaret Mitchell's Georgia heroine is also Southern, but from a Civil War novel, not Lee's.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Tom Sawyer: Twain's boy from Missouri shares Tom Robinson's first name but has no courtroom drama.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Becky Thatcher: Tom Sawyer's sweetheart in Twain's Missouri has nothing to do with Maycomb.
Characters in To Kill a Mockingbird.Pip: Dickens's orphan is from Victorian England, not 1930s Alabama.

Foods made from corn.Popcorn: Popcorn pops when water inside the kernel turns to steam and bursts the hull at roughly 180 degrees Celsius.
Foods made from corn.Grits: Grits are ground dried corn, a Southern US staple with roots in Native American cooking.
Foods made from corn.Polenta: Polenta is boiled cornmeal from northern Italy; before corn arrived from the Americas it was made from other grains.
Foods made from corn.Bourbon: To be labeled bourbon, American whiskey must be at least 51 percent corn and aged in new charred oak.
Foods made from corn.Tamale: Tamales are masa steamed in corn husks or banana leaves, a dish with roots thousands of years deep in Mesoamerica.
Foods made from corn.Tortilla chips: The corn for tortilla chips is first soaked in lime, a process called nixtamalization that unlocks its niacin.
Foods made from corn.Hominy: Hominy is corn soaked in an alkali, which swells the kernels and makes the nutrient niacin available.
Foods made from corn.Fritos: Fritos, from the 1930s, are among the simplest snacks, made from just corn, oil and salt.
Foods made from corn.Arepa: Arepas are griddled cornmeal cakes eaten daily in Venezuela and Colombia, usually split and stuffed.
Foods made from corn.Cheetos: Cheetos are puffed, extruded cornmeal dusted with cheese powder; the first ones came out in 1948.
Foods made from corn.Elote: Elote is Mexican street corn, grilled on the cob and slathered with mayo, cheese, chili and lime.
Foods made from corn.Couscous: Couscous looks like a grain, but it is tiny steamed pasta rolled from semolina, which is durum wheat.
Foods made from corn.Pasta: Pasta is traditionally durum wheat semolina, not corn, though corn-based versions are popular in gluten-free diets.
Foods made from corn.Oatmeal: Oatmeal comes from oats, a different cereal; it shares only the grass family with corn.
Foods made from corn.Potato chips: Potato chips are sliced potatoes, and legend credits chef George Crum with inventing them in 1853.
Foods made from corn.Bagel: Bagels are wheat dough boiled before baking, which gives them their chew and glossy crust.
Foods made from corn.Quinoa: Quinoa is a seed from a plant related to spinach, grown in the Andes, and is not a grass like corn.
Foods made from corn.Sake: Sake is brewed from rice, a process closer to beer than to whiskey, because starch is converted to sugar by mold.
Foods made from corn.Scotch whisky: Scotch is built on malted barley; unlike bourbon, corn is not required, though some grain whiskies use it.
Foods made from corn.Pretzel: Pretzels are wheat dough dipped in lye before baking, which gives the shiny brown crust.
Foods made from corn.Croissant: Croissants are wheat dough layered with butter into dozens of flaky sheets, an Austrian kipferl reinvented in France.
Foods made from corn.Rice cake: Puffed rice cakes are made by heating rice grains under pressure until they explode into discs.
Foods made from corn.Bulgur: Bulgur is cracked, parboiled wheat, the base of Middle Eastern tabbouleh.
Foods made from corn.Hash browns: Hash browns are grated, fried potatoes, and the name comes from the old word 'hash' meaning chopped.

Living things.Mushroom: Mushrooms are the fruiting bodies of fungi, which are closer relatives to animals than to plants.
Living things.Moss: Moss has no roots or flowers, and many species can dry out completely and revive when water returns.
Living things.Coral: Coral is an animal, and reefs cover less than one percent of the sea floor but shelter about a quarter of marine species.
Living things.Yeast: Yeast is a single-celled fungus, and one species, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, both brews beer and raises bread.
Living things.Bacteria: Your body hosts roughly as many bacterial cells as human ones, and most of them are harmless or helpful.
Living things.Sea sponge: Sea sponges are animals with no nerves or organs, and they are among the earliest animals on Earth.
Living things.Lichen: Lichen is a partnership between a fungus and an alga, and some patches grow only millimeters a year and live for centuries.
Living things.Algae: Algae produce a large share of Earth's oxygen, and some, like phytoplankton, are single cells.
Living things.Oak tree: A single oak can support hundreds of species of insects, birds and fungi.
Living things.Seaweed: Seaweed is algae, not a plant, and giant kelp can grow about half a meter in a day.
Living things.Barnacle: Barnacles are crustaceans related to crabs, and they glue themselves head-first to rocks and ship hulls for life.
Living things.Mold: Mold is a fungus, and the mold Penicillium gave us the first antibiotic, discovered in 1928.
Living things.Pearl: A pearl forms when an oyster coats an irritant in layers of nacre, but the finished pearl is not alive.
Living things.Fire: Fire consumes fuel, grows and spreads, but it is a chemical reaction with no cells, so it isn't alive.
Living things.Crystal: Crystals can grow in repeating patterns, but they have no cells or metabolism, so they aren't alive.
Living things.Cloud: Clouds form and drift, but they are only droplets of water or ice, not living things.
Living things.Amber: Amber is fossilized tree resin, and it sometimes preserves insects that are tens of millions of years old.
Living things.Fossil: A fossil is the remains or traces of a once-living thing turned to stone, but the fossil itself is not alive.
Living things.Coal: Coal is the compressed remains of ancient swamp plants, mostly from the Carboniferous period.
Living things.Kitchen sponge: A kitchen sponge is cellulose or foam, but it can harbor billions of bacteria; the living kind is the sea sponge.
Living things.Robot: The word robot comes from Czech 'robota', meaning forced labor, from the 1920 play R.U.R., and robots are not alive.
Living things.Seashell: A seashell is calcium carbonate built by a mollusk, and once the animal is gone, it is empty and nonliving.
Living things.Stalactite: Stalactites grow downward from cave ceilings as minerals drip, often only a fraction of a millimeter a year.
Living things.Petrified wood: In petrified wood, minerals like silica replaced the plant's cells over millions of years, so it's now stone.

Things moved or powered by wind.Sailboat: A sailboat can travel faster than the wind that powers it, by angling its sails like wings and sailing across the breeze.
Things moved or powered by wind.Windmill: The first known windmills, in Persia around the 9th century, used vertical sails to grind grain.
Things moved or powered by wind.Kite: Kites were invented in China over 2,000 years ago, and early ones were used for measuring and signaling.
Things moved or powered by wind.Wind turbine: The blades of the largest offshore wind turbines exceed 100 meters, longer than a football field.
Things moved or powered by wind.Pinwheel: A pinwheel spins because wind pressing on its angled vanes creates a turning force, just like a turbine.
Things moved or powered by wind.Windsurfer: Windsurfing became an Olympic sport in 1984 and combines a surfboard with a handheld sail.
Things moved or powered by wind.Wind chime: Japanese glass wind bells, called furin, are hung in summer, and their tinkle is meant to feel cooling.
Things moved or powered by wind.Weather vane: A weather vane points to where the wind is coming from, not where it is going.
Things moved or powered by wind.Land yacht: Land yachts are wheeled sail-powered vehicles, and one called Greenbird set a record of over 200 km/h.
Things moved or powered by wind.Iceboat: Iceboats can reach several times the speed of the wind pushing them, because there's so little friction on ice.
Things moved or powered by wind.Rowboat: A rowboat runs on arm and back power alone, and rowing is among the oldest ways to travel on water.
Things moved or powered by wind.Canoe: The word canoe comes from a Caribbean word 'kanoa', and canoes are propelled by paddles.
Things moved or powered by wind.Bicycle: A bicycle runs on your muscles, and nearly all of your pedaling effort turns into motion.
Things moved or powered by wind.Motorboat: A motorboat's engine burns fuel to turn a propeller, no wind involved.
Things moved or powered by wind.Paddle board: Stand-up paddleboarding, popularized in Hawaii, is powered by a paddle, not wind.
Things moved or powered by wind.Skateboard: A skateboard moves by pushing off with your foot, or by gravity on slopes.
Things moved or powered by wind.Water wheel: A water wheel is powered by flowing water and was used for grinding grain thousands of years ago.
Things moved or powered by wind.Steam engine: Thomas Newcomen's steam engine of 1712 burned coal to pump water from mines, no wind needed.
Things moved or powered by wind.Solar panel: Solar panels use sunlight, but wind itself comes from the sun, since the sun's uneven heating of air creates it.
Things moved or powered by wind.Car: A car burns fuel or draws battery power, and moves independent of the wind.
Things moved or powered by wind.Rocket: A rocket works by throwing exhaust backward, so it works even in the vacuum of space where there is no wind.
Things moved or powered by wind.Pedal boat: A pedal boat runs on leg power, a paddle wheel driven by your pedaling.
Things moved or powered by wind.Hand fan: A hand fan creates wind rather than using it, a neat reversal.
Things moved or powered by wind.Treadmill: The treadmill was invented in 1818 as a prison punishment device, with inmates grinding grain.

Things usually sold in a can.Tuna: Canned tuna is cooked inside the can after sealing, and in the US it is called the most commonly eaten fish.
Things usually sold in a can.Soda: The pull-tab was invented in 1959, and the modern stay-on tab replaced loose rings that littered beaches.
Things usually sold in a can.Baked beans: Canned baked beans were popularized by Heinz, and the 'baked' is a bit generous since they are usually steam cooked.
Things usually sold in a can.Spam: Spam launched in 1937, and Hawaiians eat more per person than anywhere in the US, using it in sushi-style musubi.
Things usually sold in a can.House paint: Paint is sold in cans that are sealed with a friction lid, so you pry it open with a flat screwdriver.
Things usually sold in a can.Sardines: Sardines come in cans because they spoil quickly, and canning them became a big industry in Europe in the 1800s.
Things usually sold in a can.Cat food: Canned cat food is popular partly because it provides moisture that cats, descended from desert animals, drink little of.
Things usually sold in a can.Spray paint: Spray paint's aerosol can contains a small ball that rattles; the marble helps mix the pigment.
Things usually sold in a can.Tennis balls: Tennis balls are sold in pressurized cans, which keeps them bouncy until you open the can.
Things usually sold in a can.Condensed milk: Condensed milk is sweetened and has about 60 percent of its water removed, and it can last for years.
Things usually sold in a can.Coconut milk: Coconut milk is not the water inside the nut; it's made by pressing grated coconut flesh with water.
Things usually sold in a can.Tomato paste: Tomato paste is a concentrated puree, and it takes several pounds of tomatoes to make one can.
Things usually sold in a can.Bread: Bread is sold in bags or loaves, since a can would make it soggy, though some brown bread is canned.
Things usually sold in a can.Eggs: Eggs are sold in cartons, and their shell protects them so no can is needed.
Things usually sold in a can.Milk: Milk is normally sold in cartons or jugs, and canned versions exist only as evaporated or condensed.
Things usually sold in a can.Cereal: Cereal comes in boxes with liners to stay crisp, and a can would crush the flakes.
Things usually sold in a can.Yogurt: Yogurt comes in tubs or cups, because live cultures would be killed by the high heat of canning.
Things usually sold in a can.Rice: Rice is typically sold in bags, and it stays good for years when dry.
Things usually sold in a can.Cheese: Cheese is usually in blocks or wrappers, but a canned cheese is a classic in some places.
Things usually sold in a can.Ice cream: Ice cream goes in tubs or cartons, since it needs a freezer, which a can can't give.
Things usually sold in a can.Ketchup: Ketchup is sold in bottles and its glass or plastic design helps it pour slowly, a trait sometimes joked about.
Things usually sold in a can.Honey: Honey is sold in jars or squeeze bottles, and sealed honey can stay edible for a very long time.
Things usually sold in a can.Lettuce: Lettuce is sold fresh or bagged, as it wilts and goes mushy under canning heat.
Things usually sold in a can.Flour: Flour is sold in paper bags, and it is flammable as dust, so mills have a real explosion risk.

Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Great Hall: The dining hall's ceiling is enchanted to look like the sky outside, and the feasts are served by house-elves.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Room of Requirement: It appears only when someone truly needs it, and it became the meeting place of Dumbledore's Army.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Gryffindor Tower: The common room is behind the Fat Lady's portrait, and the password changes regularly.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Chamber of Secrets: Salazar Slytherin built the hidden chamber, entered through a girls' bathroom, to hold his basilisk.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Astronomy Tower: The tallest tower at Hogwarts is where astronomy lessons are held, and it's the scene of Dumbledore's death.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Hospital Wing: Madam Pomfrey runs the infirmary and can heal broken bones overnight, though regrowing them is unpleasant.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Owlery: A tower where school owls live, and where students send letters, including Hedwig's post for Harry.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Quidditch pitch: The grounds' pitch has three tall hoops at each end, and the game ends when a Seeker catches the Golden Snitch.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Restricted Section: The library's forbidden section holds dark magic books and requires a signed note from a teacher to enter.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Trophy Room: This hall holds awards and memorabilia, including a Special Award for Services to the School for Tom Riddle.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Dumbledore's office: Entering requires a password, often named after a sweet, and it is guarded by a stone gargoyle.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Diagon Alley: It's the London shopping street for wizards, not part of Hogwarts, and it's entered through the Leaky Cauldron.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Gringotts: The wizarding bank is in London, run by goblins and guarded by dragons deep underground.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Leaky Cauldron: A London pub whose back wall opens into Diagon Alley; it's not part of the school.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Ministry of Magic: The wizarding government is hidden beneath London, and its visitors arrive through a red phone box.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Azkaban: The wizard prison sits on an island in the North Sea, guarded by Dementors.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Godric's Hollow: This village is where Harry's parents were killed and where Godric Gryffindor was born, but it's nowhere near the castle.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.The Burrow: The Weasleys' crooked home near Ottery St Catchpole is not at Hogwarts.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Hogsmeade: The all-wizarding village is close to the castle but outside the grounds, and students may visit only from third year with permission.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Shrieking Shack: The 'most haunted' hut in Hogsmeade is outside school grounds; its screams were really Remus Lupin's werewolf transformations, not ghosts.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Privet Drive: The Dursleys' home in Surrey is where Harry spent his childhood, and it isn't part of Hogwarts.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Spinner's End: Snape's childhood home is in a run-down mill town, far from Hogwarts.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Knockturn Alley: A dark side street off Diagon Alley that sells shady magical items, away from the castle.
Places inside Hogwarts castle or grounds.Grimmauld Place: This is the Black family's London house that became the Order of the Phoenix headquarters, located in London and not Hogwarts.

Fibonacci numbers.1: The sequence starts with two 1s, and each number afterward is the sum of the two before it.
Fibonacci numbers.2: The only even prime number also appears in the Fibonacci sequence, right after the two 1s.
Fibonacci numbers.3: Fibonacci's third number, and the first Fibonacci number that is also prime besides 2.
Fibonacci numbers.4: Four skips the sequence; it falls between 3 and 5, and breaks the pattern since 2 plus 3 is 5.
Fibonacci numbers.5: Five is a Fibonacci number; many flowers, like buttercups, have five petals, a classic example.
Fibonacci numbers.6: Six is the smallest perfect number, but the sequence jumps from 5 to 8.
Fibonacci numbers.7: Seven is missing from Fibonacci, though the ratio of 8 to 5 is close to the golden ratio.
Fibonacci numbers.8: Eight is the only Fibonacci number besides 1 that is a perfect cube.
Fibonacci numbers.9: Nine is not a Fibonacci number; it falls between 8 and 13.
Fibonacci numbers.10: Ten is no Fibonacci number, though the sum 5 + 5 might trick you; the sequence goes 8, 13.
Fibonacci numbers.12: Twelve sits between 8 and 13 and isn't a Fibonacci number.
Fibonacci numbers.13: Thirteen is the seventh Fibonacci number, and a prime, and the baker's dozen.
Fibonacci numbers.14: Fourteen is close to 13, but isn't a Fibonacci number.
Fibonacci numbers.21: Twenty-one is the eighth Fibonacci number, and a blackjack total.
Fibonacci numbers.22: Twenty-two is only one more than 21, and not a Fibonacci number.
Fibonacci numbers.34: Thirty-four sits in the sequence, and the ratio of 34 to 21 is already close to the golden ratio, about 1.618.
Fibonacci numbers.35: Thirty-five is just past 34, and isn't in the sequence.
Fibonacci numbers.50: Fifty is a round number, not a Fibonacci one; 55 is the next one.
Fibonacci numbers.55: Fifty-five is also a triangular number, the sum of 1 through 10.
Fibonacci numbers.89: Eighty-nine is a Fibonacci prime, and 1/89 has digits that sum the Fibonacci numbers in disguise.
Fibonacci numbers.100: One hundred misses; the sequence goes 89, 144.
Fibonacci numbers.144: The largest Fibonacci number that is a perfect square except 1, and a gross.
Fibonacci numbers.150: One hundred fifty is just above 144, which is Fibonacci, while 150 isn't.
Fibonacci numbers.233: Two hundred thirty-three is a Fibonacci prime, which is the 13th number in the sequence.

Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Partridge: First printed in England in 1780 in a children's book as a memory-and-forfeit game, where players had to recite the gifts without a slip.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Pear tree: The first day's gift is a whole tree. The partridge sits in it, and pear trees can live for decades.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Turtle doves: "Turtle" here comes from Latin turtur, imitating the bird's soft call. It's nothing to do with reptiles, and the species is now in steep decline in Europe.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.French hens: Three on day three, repeated on each of the later days, so by the end you'd have 30 of them.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Calling birds: Probably first "colly birds," an old word for blackbirds, since colly meant coal-black. "Calling" is a later change.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Gold rings: Five on day five. Because every other bird gift is a bird, some argue it meant ring-necked pheasants.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Geese: Six a-laying. A goose egg is more than twice the size of a chicken egg, so that's a lot of omelet.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Swans: Seven a-swimming. In England, unmarked mute swans on open water belong to the Crown by tradition.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Maids milking: Eight milkmaids. Their reputation for clear skin helped inspire Edward Jenner's smallpox vaccine.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Ladies dancing: Nine on day nine. In the annual PNC Christmas Price Index, they're among the costliest gifts.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Lords a-leaping: Ten a-leaping. In the PNC Christmas Price Index, they're usually the single priciest item.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Pipers: Eleven pipers close the song with the drummers, so the final two gifts of the song are musicians.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Drummers: Twelve drumming. With every repeat, the song delivers 364 gifts, almost one for every day of the year.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Reindeer: Not in the song. Santa's reindeer first appear in the 1823 poem A Visit from St. Nicholas, a different story.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Sleigh bells: Not in the song. Jingle Bells (1857) was the first song broadcast from space, by Gemini 6 in 1965.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Snowmen: Not in the song. Frosty the Snowman is from a 1950 song and later a cartoon, nothing to do with the twelve days.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Angels: Not in the song. They sing in carols like Hark! The Herald Angels Sing, though not here.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Wise men: Not in the song, but the twelve days end on the eve of Epiphany, which celebrates the arrival of the wise men.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Shepherds: Not in the song. They belong to the nativity story, visited by angels, and have no verse here.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Candy canes: Not in the song. Candy canes are a modern treat, and the J-shape-as-shepherd-crook story is legend.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Elves: Not in the song. Santa's elf helpers are mostly a Victorian-era idea, not an old Twelve Days gift.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Stockings: Not in the song. In the legend of Saint Nicholas, gold coins landed in stockings drying by the fire.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Chestnuts: Not in the song. They're roasting in Mel Torme's 1945 "The Christmas Song," a different carol.
Gifts in The Twelve Days of Christmas.Mistletoe: Not in the song. In Norse myth, the god Baldr was killed by a sprig of it, a darker origin for the kissing custom.

Symphony orchestra instruments.Violin: Stradivarius violins from Cremona, made in the 1600s and 1700s, can fetch millions of dollars for their tone.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Viola: Slightly larger and deeper than a violin, it reads alto clef, which almost no other instrument uses.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Cello: Played between the knees, it covers nearly the range of the human voice, resting on an endpin since the 19th century.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Double bass: The largest and lowest orchestral string instrument; it descends from the viol family rather than the violin family.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Flute: Orchestral flutes are metal, yet classed as woodwinds because they were once made of wood.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Oboe: The orchestra tunes to the oboe's A, because its pitch is steady and cuts through the sound.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Clarinet: Invented around 1700 by Johann Denner in Germany, and loved by Mozart.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Bassoon: A double-reed instrument whose tube is about 2.6 meters long folded back on itself.
Symphony orchestra instruments.French horn: Its coiled tubing would stretch to about 3.7 meters if straightened; the 'French' label is a historical quirk.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Trumpet: Trumpets were found in Tutankhamun's tomb; valves only arrived in the 1800s.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Trombone: Its slide lets players glide between pitches; the name means 'big trumpet' in Italian.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Tuba: The lowest brass instrument, with tubing that can run to around 5 meters.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Timpani: Kettledrums with pedals that change pitch, among the few drums tuned to specific notes.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Harp: A concert harp has 47 strings and seven pedals.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Piccolo: Half the size of a flute, sounding an octave higher, it's the highest orchestral woodwind.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Guitar: Orchestras rarely include one, though Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez makes it a soloist.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Banjo: Descended from West African instruments and shaped by enslaved Africans in America; not a standard orchestra member.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Accordion: A free-reed instrument invented in early 19th-century Vienna; rare in orchestras.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Drum kit: Orchestral percussion is individual drums; the drum kit emerged from jazz in the early 1900s.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Electric bass: Leo Fender's 1951 Precision Bass; in an orchestra the double bass fills that role.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Mandolin: Occasionally appears in Mahler's symphonies, but isn't a regular orchestra member.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Bagpipes: A Scottish instrument with a bag and drones, not part of the orchestra.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Ukulele: Hawaii's adaptation of a Portuguese instrument in the 1880s; the name is often translated as 'jumping flea'.
Symphony orchestra instruments.Harmonica: Vaughan Williams wrote a Romance for harmonica and orchestra in 1951, but it is not a standard member.
